ChroTel: ChroTel (Chromospheric Telescope) is a ground-based robotic full-disk solar telescope at Observatorio del Teide, Tenerife, Spain, with routine synoptic operation from 2012 after 2008 commissioning. It images the solar chromosphere in H-alpha, Ca II K, and He I 10830 Å for studies of filaments, plages, coronal holes, and solar activity.
EUNIS: EUNIS is a NASA sounding-rocket solar spectrograph flown from White Sands Missile Range on suborbital flights since 2006, with solar campaigns including 2006, 2007, 2013, and 2021. It spends only minutes above the atmosphere per flight, observing high-resolution extreme-ultraviolet spectra/images of the chromosphere, transition region, and corona and calibrating space EUV instruments.
Evans: The John W. Evans Solar Facility at Sacramento Peak/Sunspot, New Mexico, is a ground-based NSO solar observatory that began operation in 1952. Its spectroheliograph/coronagraph observations provide narrowband full-disk and off-limb solar images of the chromosphere, photosphere, and corona for studies of solar atmospheric structure and activity; no orbital phase applies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Pioneer10: NASA’s Pioneer 10 (launched 1972; routine mission ended 1997, last contact 2003) was a deep-space planetary and heliophysics probe. It cruised outward through the inner solar system and asteroid belt in 1972-73, flew through Jupiter’s magnetosphere during the Dec. 1973 flyby, then followed a solar-system escape trajectory through the outer heliosphere, measuring solar wind, magnetic fields, cosmic rays, and energetic particles.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Helios2: Helios 2 (Helios-B) was a West German/NASA solar probe launched in 1976 and operated until 1980. It remained throughout the mission in a highly elliptical, near-ecliptic heliocentric orbit from about 0.29 AU perihelion to near 1 AU aphelion, measuring inner-heliospheric solar wind plasma, magnetic fields, energetic particles, radio/plasma waves, and dust.
FOXSI1: FOXSI-1 (Focusing Optics X-ray Solar Imager flight 1) was a NASA sounding-rocket solar mission launched and completed on 2012-11-02 from White Sands Missile Range. It followed a single suborbital ballistic trajectory above Earth’s atmosphere, not an Earth orbit, providing minutes of solar pointing to demonstrate focusing hard-X-ray imaging spectroscopy of active regions and microflares.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/1S: BARREL-1S was a NASA Balloon Array for RBSP Relativistic Electron Losses payload launched in 2013 for the Antarctic BARREL campaign and ended in 2013. It was not an orbiter: carried by a stratospheric balloon at roughly 30–40 km in the Antarctic polar vortex, it measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, with magnetometer/housekeeping context, in conjunction with the Van Allen Probes.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/1I: BARREL-1I was a single NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for RBSP Relativistic Electron Losses stratospheric balloon payload operated in the 2013 Antarctic long-duration balloon campaign. It drifted at high altitude over Antarctica/Southern Ocean rather than orbiting, carrying X-ray scintillator and magnetometer measurements of radiation-belt electron precipitation and magnetospheric coupling.
SATech-01: SATech-01, launched in 2022, is a Chinese solar remote-sensing satellite in low Earth Sun-synchronous orbit; no major orbital phase changes are reported. Its Solar Upper Transition Region Imager (SUTRI) takes full-disk extreme-ultraviolet images, especially around 46.5 nm, to study the Sun’s upper chromosphere, transition region, corona, and space-weather-relevant activity.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/DMSP_5D-3/F16: DMSP F16 was a U.S. Air Force DMSP 5D-3 spacecraft launched in 2003 and operated until 2020 in a near-circular, Sun-synchronous polar low-Earth orbit at about 830–850 km altitude; its orbit type did not change. It provided operational meteorological and space-weather measurements of the high-latitude ionosphere/aurora, including SSJ precipitating particles, ionospheric plasma, and magnetic-field data.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/ISEE1: ISEE 1 (International Sun-Earth Explorer 1, 1977-1987) was a NASA magnetospheric spacecraft. It remained in a highly elliptical geocentric orbit, with apogee about 23 Earth radii and low perigee, sampling the solar wind, bow shock, magnetopause, magnetosheath, magnetotail, and inner magnetosphere with plasma, magnetic-field, energetic-particle, and wave instruments.
GONG: Global Oscillation Network Group (GONG, operational since 1995) is a six-site ground-based solar network at Big Bear, Cerro Tololo, El Teide, Learmonth, Mauna Loa, and Udaipur, providing near-continuous full-disk Doppler velocity, intensity/white-light, magnetogram, and later H-alpha observations for helioseismology and solar magnetic activity studies.
HXECLIPSE: UCAR/NCAR HAO Historical Eclipse Archive (HXECLIPSE; VSO data service, operational start not documented here) is a virtual collection of ground-based solar eclipse photographs/images from HAO historical expeditions and other sources. It has no orbit or single station: observations were made from eclipse-path sites on Earth at the dates of individual eclipses, mainly of the white-light corona.
Hi-C: Hi-C (High-resolution Coronal Imager) is a NASA sounding-rocket solar observatory, not an orbital spacecraft; it makes brief suborbital flights from White Sands Missile Range. Hi-C flew on 11 Jul 2012, obtaining ~5 min of ultra-high-resolution 193 Å EUV coronal images; Hi-C 2.1 flew on 29 May 2018 at 172 Å; Hi-C Flare flew on 17 Apr 2024 for flare/coronal EUV imaging.
Hi-C21: Hi-C 2.1 (High Resolution Coronal Imager 2.1) was a NASA suborbital sounding-rocket solar observatory launched in 2018 from White Sands Missile Range; its mission ended after the same brief ballistic flight above Earth’s atmosphere. It obtained high-spatial-resolution 172 Å EUV images of active-region coronal loops and fine solar-corona structure.
Hinode: Hinode (Solar-B), launched in 2006 and still operating, is a JAXA/NASA/UK solar observatory in a near-circular Sun-synchronous low Earth polar orbit; its orbit has not substantially changed. It observes the solar photosphere, chromosphere, transition region, and corona, measuring magnetic fields, plasma dynamics, flares, eruptions, and coronal heating with SOT, XRT, and EIS.
IRIS: NASA’s Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph (IRIS, launched 2013) is a Sun-pointing SMEX observatory in a near-polar, Sun-synchronous low-Earth orbit that has not changed over the mission. It studies the solar chromosphere and transition region with high-resolution ultraviolet spectroscopy and slit-jaw imaging, probing mass and energy flow between the photosphere and corona.
ISOON: The Improved Solar Observing Optical Network (ISOON) was a ground-based full-disk H-alpha solar telescope at the USAF/Sacramento Peak site in Sunspot, New Mexico, operating roughly from 2000 to 2013. It provided high-cadence chromospheric images and movies for monitoring flares, filaments, active regions, and space-weather-related solar activity.
KPVT: Kitt Peak Vacuum Tower Telescope (KPVT) was a ground-based full-disk solar observatory on Kitt Peak, Arizona, operated for synoptic solar magnetism from 1973 to 2003. It used the 512-channel magnetograph (to 1992) and later the spectromagnetograph (1992-2003) to measure photospheric line-of-sight magnetic fields, velocities, and related solar properties.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/DMSP_5D-3/F17: DMSP F17 was a U.S. Defense Meteorological Satellite Program 5D-3 spacecraft (launched 2006, operated to 2022) for space-weather and environmental monitoring. It remained in a near-circular Sun-synchronous polar low-Earth orbit, about 840 km altitude and 98–99° inclination, measuring auroral particle precipitation, ionospheric plasma/drifts, magnetic fields, and near-Earth geospace conditions with instruments such as SSJ/5, SSIES, and SSM.
MCCD: The Mees CCD Imaging Spectrograph (MCCD), operating circa 1992–2009 at the University of Hawaii’s Mees Solar Observatory on Haleakala, Maui, was a ground-based solar imaging spectrograph. It observed from a fixed terrestrial site, recording CCD chromospheric and photospheric spectral line profiles for studies of active regions, flares, and the solar atmosphere.
MINXSS1: MinXSS-1 (Miniature X-Ray Solar Spectrometer, launched to the ISS in 2015, deployed 2016, reentered 2017) was a 3U CubeSat solar irradiance mission. From May 2016 to May 2017 it operated in low Earth orbit after ISS deployment, measuring solar soft X-ray spectral irradiance with the X123 silicon drift detector for flares, active regions, and irradiance variability.
MLSO: Mauna Loa Solar Observatory (MLSO, operational since 1965) is a ground-based solar observatory on Mauna Loa, Hawaii, providing synoptic daytime observations of the solar chromosphere and low corona. It measures coronal white-light brightness/polarization and chromospheric/He I features for solar and heliospheric studies, with instruments including the Mk3/Mk4 and K-Cor coronagraphs.
McMath: McMath–Pierce Solar Telescope at Kitt Peak, Arizona, was a ground-based solar observatory operated from 1962 to 2017. It provided high-resolution visible and infrared observations of the Sun, especially spectroscopy of the photosphere, chromosphere, and sunspots; its Fourier Transform Spectrometer produced widely used detailed solar spectra.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/LANL/1990: LANL-1990 was a Los Alamos National Laboratory geosynchronous spacecraft operating from 1990 to 2004. It remained in geosynchronous Earth orbit and carried MPA and SOPA instruments to measure magnetospheric plasma and energetic particle populations, supporting studies of the radiation belts, ring current, substorms, and space weather.
MtWilson: Mount Wilson Observatory is a ground-based solar observatory on Mount Wilson, California, with solar operations beginning in 1908. Its 60-ft Solar Tower spectroheliograph provides synoptic full-disk chromospheric solar images, especially H-alpha and Ca II K, for studies of sunspots, plages, filaments, active regions, and long-term solar activity; it has no spacecraft orbit.
OACT: INAF–Osservatorio Astrofisico di Catania (OACT), a ground-based observatory in Catania, Sicily, Italy, has carried out solar observations since the late 19th century (founded 1880). Its VSO solar data are optical full-disk photospheric continuum/white-light and Hα chromospheric images used to monitor sunspots, plages, filaments, flares, and other solar activity.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/ISIS2: ISIS 2 (International Satellites for Ionospheric Studies) was a Canadian/NASA topside-ionosphere satellite launched in 1971 and operated until 1990. It remained in a near-circular, near-polar low Earth orbit at about 1,350–1,420 km altitude and 88° inclination. It measured ionospheric electron density, plasma waves, particles, and auroral emissions; its SFS swept-frequency sounder produced topside ionograms.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/LANL/1994: LANL-1994, a Los Alamos National Laboratory geosynchronous spacecraft operational from 1994 to 2007, observed Earth’s inner magnetosphere from near geostationary orbit; its orbit did not change. It supported space-weather and magnetospheric studies with instruments such as MPA and SOPA measuring thermal plasma, energetic particles, and radiation-belt populations.
OBSPM: Observatoire de Paris’s Département d’Astronomie Solaire at Meudon, France, is a ground-based solar observatory, with spectroheliograph operations dating from 1909 and continuing in modern form. It records full-disk solar spectroheliograms in lines such as H-alpha, Ca II K, and Ca II 8542 for chromospheric/photospheric structure, filaments, plages, prominences, and solar activity studies.
OMP: Pic-du-Midi Observatory (OMP), founded in 1882, is a ground-based high-altitude solar observatory on Pic du Midi de Bigorre in the French Pyrenees, France. Its modern CLIMSO solar patrol has operated since 2007, imaging the solar disk, prominences, and low corona in white light and selected chromospheric/coronal lines such as H-alpha and Ca II for solar activity studies.
OVRO: Owens Valley Radio Observatory is a Caltech ground-based radio facility near Big Pine, California, operating since 1956. For heliophysics it hosts the Owens Valley Solar Array, expanded as EOVSA in 2017, which makes solar microwave/radio interferometric images and spectra for studies of flares, coronal magnetic fields, and energetic electrons.
GOES17: NOAA’s GOES-17 (launched 2018; GOES-West service ended 2023) is a geostationary space-weather/solar observatory carrying SUVI, EXIS, SEISS and MAG for coronal EUV imaging, solar X-ray/EUV irradiance, particles and fields. It was checked out near 89.5°W in 2018, operated at ~137.2°W from late 2018/Feb 2019 to Jan 2023, then drifted to ~104.7°W as an on-orbit spare.
PROBA2: ESA’s PROBA2 (launched 2009) is a technology-demonstration microsatellite that has remained in low-Earth Sun-synchronous orbit. It supports solar and space-weather science, observing solar EUV coronal emission with SWAP and solar irradiance/flare variability with the LYRA radiometer, with additional in-situ plasma instruments for the near-Earth environment.
PSP: NASA’s Parker Solar Probe (launched 2018) studies the solar corona, solar-wind origin, magnetic fields, plasma, energetic particles, and inner-heliospheric white-light structure. From 2018-2024 it used repeated Venus gravity assists to shrink a highly elliptical heliocentric orbit with progressively closer perihelia and some Venus-flyby science; from late 2024 onward it flies its final close solar orbit, reaching about 9.9 solar radii.
RHESSI: RHESSI (Reuven Ramaty High Energy Solar Spectroscopic Imager) was a NASA SMEX mission launched in 2002 and operated until 2018. It remained in low-Earth orbit throughout the mission, a roughly 600 km, 38° inclination orbit that gradually decayed. RHESSI used rotating modulation collimators and germanium detectors to image and spectroscopically measure solar-flare hard X-ray and gamma-ray emission.
SDO: NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO, launched 2010) is a heliophysics mission in an inclined geosynchronous Earth orbit (near 102°W longitude, 24-hour period); its observing orbit has not changed over the mission. SDO provides near-continuous full-disk solar observations with AIA EUV/UV imaging, HMI magnetic/helioseismic measurements, and EVE solar EUV irradiance.
SFT: Solar Flare Telescope (SFT, operational from 1990) is a ground-based solar observatory at the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan in Mitaka, Tokyo. It observes the full solar disk, chiefly in H-alpha, to study chromospheric flares, filaments, prominences, and eruption morphology; it also supports photospheric magnetic-field context for solar activity studies.
SMM: NASA’s Solar Maximum Mission (SMM, 1980-1989) was a Sun-pointed observatory in low Earth orbit for solar-flare, coronal, and irradiance studies. It remained in LEO throughout; after an attitude-control failure in 1980 it operated in a degraded mode until Shuttle repair and redeployment in 1984. Instruments included the Coronagraph/Polarimeter, hard X-ray and gamma-ray spectrometers, and irradiance monitors.
SO: Solar Orbiter (ESA/NASA, launched 2020) studies solar atmosphere, solar wind, magnetic fields, energetic particles and the heliosphere with remote-sensing and in-situ instruments. It spent 2020-21 in cruise/commissioning heliocentric orbit with Venus gravity assists and a Nov. 2021 Earth flyby; since late 2021 it has followed a Venus-resonant eccentric science orbit with perihelia down to ~0.28 AU, with later Venus flybys raising inclination for polar views.
SOLIS: SOLIS (Synoptic Optical Long-term Investigations of the Sun) was an NSO ground-based synoptic solar observatory operating at Kitt Peak, Arizona, from 2003 to 2017. It obtained full-disk photospheric magnetic-field and Doppler measurements plus chromospheric and spectral irradiance observations with VSM, ISS, and Full Disk Patrol.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/1T: BARREL-1T was a Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses test high-altitude balloon payload, operated during the 2008-2009 Antarctic long-duration balloon season and ending in 2009. It was not in orbit; it floated in the stratosphere over Antarctica/Southern Ocean on circumpolar winds, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays/gamma rays and magnetic perturbations from radiation-belt electron precipitation.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/1C: BARREL-1C was a NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses payload flown over Antarctica in 2013. It was a stratospheric long-duration balloon, not a spacecraft, drifting at high altitude over the Antarctic polar region to measure bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, plus magnetic-field/ULF-wave context for magnetospheric loss studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/4G: BARREL-4G was a NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses payload operated in the fourth Antarctic long-duration-balloon campaign (2015-2016). It drifted in the stratosphere over Antarctica, not in space orbit, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation to study magnetospheric wave-particle interactions and atmospheric loss.
TRACE: NASA’s Transition Region and Coronal Explorer (TRACE; launched 1998, operated until 2010) was a solar SMEX observatory in a near-circular, Sun-synchronous low-Earth polar orbit throughout its mission. It obtained high-resolution normal-incidence EUV, UV, and white-light images of the solar transition region and corona, studying coronal loops, active regions, flares, and solar magnetic dynamics.
VAULT: VAULT/VAULT2.0 is a NASA sounding-rocket ultraviolet solar telescope, not an orbital observatory. Original VAULT suborbital flights from White Sands occurred in 1999 and 2002; the upgraded VAULT2.0 flew in 2014, with operations ending after each minutes-long flight. It obtained very high angular resolution H I Lyman-alpha 1216 Å solar images of the upper chromosphere and transition region.
YOHKOH: Yohkoh (Solar-A) was Japan’s ISAS solar X-ray observatory, launched in 1991; routine science ended after attitude-control loss in December 2001, and it reentered in 2005. It remained in a near-circular low Earth orbit (~600 km altitude, ~31° inclination) throughout its mission, observing solar flares, coronal heating, and high-energy plasma with SXT, HXT, BCS, and WBS.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ulysses: Ulysses was a joint ESA/NASA mission (1990-2009) studying the heliosphere in 3D. After launch it cruised in the ecliptic to Jupiter, making a February 1992 Jovian flyby with magnetospheric science, then entered a high-inclination heliocentric orbit for solar polar passes in 1994-95, 2000-01, and 2006-08, measuring solar wind plasma/composition, fields, energetic particles, and radio/plasma waves.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/IMAGE: NASA’s IMAGE (Imager for Magnetopause-to-Aurora Global Exploration, 2000-2005) was a spin-stabilized spacecraft in a highly elliptical near-polar Earth orbit throughout its science mission, enabling global magnetospheric imaging. It observed the plasmasphere, ring current, aurora, magnetopause, and cusp using FUV/EUV imagers, energetic neutral atom imagers, and the Radio Plasma Imager.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/POLAR: NASA’s POLAR spacecraft (1996-2008) studied Earth’s polar magnetosphere, aurora, plasma, fields, waves, and energetic particles. It remained in a highly elliptical, near-polar geocentric orbit (about 1.8 by 9 Earth radii, 18-hr period); orbital precession shifted apogee viewing/coverage through different polar and magnetospheric regions over the mission.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Wind: NASA’s Wind spacecraft (launched 1994) studies solar wind plasma, magnetic fields, energetic particles, and radio/plasma waves. From 1994 to 2004 it flew evolving highly elliptical Earth orbits with lunar swingbys, magnetosphere/radiation-belt crossings, and deep magnetotail excursions; since 2004 it has operated in a halo orbit around Sun–Earth L1 monitoring the upstream solar wind.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/CANOPUS: CANOPUS (Canadian Auroral Network for the OPEN Program Unified Study) was a Canadian ground-based auroral/geospace observatory network operated from 1986 to 2005 across subauroral and auroral latitudes in Canada. Its magnetometers, riometers, photometers, and all-sky imagers measured magnetic pulsations, cosmic-noise absorption, auroral emissions, and ionospheric activity; the magnetometer network continued as CARISMA.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Dikson: Dikson Geophysical Observatory is a high-latitude Arctic ground station at Dikson, Russia, established in 1933 and used for geomagnetic monitoring rather than spaceflight. It records ground magnetic-field variations with magnetometers to study auroral-zone ionospheric currents, geomagnetic storms, substorms, and magnetospheric dynamics.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/ParkerSolarProb: NASA’s Parker Solar Probe (launched 2018) is an ongoing heliophysics mission measuring coronal and inner-heliospheric fields, plasma, energetic particles and imaging (FIELDS, SWEAP, IS☉IS, WISPR). It has always been in a highly elliptical heliocentric orbit; Venus flybys in 2018, 2019, 2020, Feb/Oct 2021, 2023 and 2024 progressively lowered perihelion. Since late 2024 it reaches closest ~9.86 solar-radii perihelia.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Interball-1: Interball-1 (Tail Probe) was a Russian-led heliophysics spacecraft (1995-2000) that studied solar wind–magnetosphere coupling, plasma waves, particles and fields in the bow shock, magnetosheath, magnetopause and magnetotail. It remained in a highly elliptical geocentric orbit throughout the mission (about 1,000 x 190,000 km, ~63° inclination, ~4-day period), with apogee precession sampling different local times.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/MESSENGER: NASA's MESSENGER (2004-2015) studied Mercury's surface, exosphere, magnetic field, magnetosphere, and solar-wind interaction. It cruised in heliocentric orbit from 2004-2011, with Earth (2005), Venus (2006, 2007), and Mercury flybys (2008, 2008, 2009) returning science, then orbited Mercury in a highly eccentric near-polar orbit from March 2011 until impact in April 2015.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/ACE: ACE (Advanced Composition Explorer, launched 1997) is a heliophysics and space-weather mission measuring upstream solar wind plasma, magnetic field, ion and isotope composition, and energetic particles. After launch and transfer, it entered a halo/Lissajous orbit about the Sun-Earth L1 point in 1997 and has remained there; flagship instruments include MAG, SWEPAM, SWICS, ACE-EPAM, SIS, and CRIS.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/NewHorizons: New Horizons (launched 2006) is a NASA Pluto-Kuiper Belt/heliophysics spacecraft on a solar-escape heliocentric trajectory. It cruised to and observed Jupiter during a 2007 gravity-assist flyby, encountered the Pluto system in July 2015, flew by Kuiper Belt object Arrokoth in January 2019, and continues outward through the Kuiper Belt/outer heliosphere. SWAP and PEPSSI measure solar wind, pickup ions, and energetic particles.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/1K: BARREL-1K was a NASA/Dartmouth high-altitude balloon payload flown in the first BARREL Antarctic campaign in 2013, with the flight ending in 2013. It drifted in the Antarctic stratosphere/polar vortex rather than orbiting Earth, at roughly 30–40 km altitude over Antarctica and the Southern Ocean, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays and magnetic fields from radiation-belt electron precipitation.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/RENU2: RENU 2 (Rocket Experiment for Neutral Upwelling 2) was a NASA sounding-rocket payload launched from Andøya, Norway, in December 2015 and ended with that suborbital flight. It traversed the auroral/cusp ionosphere for minutes, measuring thermal plasma, electric and magnetic fields, waves, and auroral emissions to study neutral upwelling and ionospheric outflow.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/IAGA/Sitka: IAGA Sitka (SIT) is a ground geomagnetic observatory operating at Sitka, Alaska since 1901. It has no orbit; it records local vector magnetic-field components and variations for studies of geomagnetic storms, auroral electrojets, and ionospheric/magnetospheric current systems as part of the global IAGA/INTERMAGNET observatory network.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/IAGA/Amderma: Amderma (IAGA code AMD) is a fixed high-latitude ground geomagnetic observatory at Amderma, Russia, with IAGA records beginning around the 1957 IGY. It measures time variations of the local magnetic field for auroral, ionospheric, and magnetospheric current-system studies; it has no orbital phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/IAGA/Arctic.Vil: Arctic Village Magnetometer (AVI), operational at least by 1995 and ongoing, is a ground geomagnetic station at Arctic Village, Alaska (~68.1°N, 145.6°W). It has no orbit; it measures local magnetic-field variations and disturbances for auroral ionosphere, magnetosphere, and space-weather studies, with IAGA/CDAWeb data.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/IAGA/Fresno: Fresno (IAGA code FRN) is a ground-based USGS geomagnetic observatory near Fresno/O’Neals, California, USA, operational since 1980. It has no orbit or changing vantage point; it continuously measures local vector geomagnetic field variations for studies of magnetic storms, ionospheric/magnetospheric currents, and secular change.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Andenes: Andenes Geophysical Observatory is a ground station at Andenes, northern Norway (about 69.3°N, 16.0°E), operational since at least the 1990s. It operates fluxgate magnetometers measuring local geomagnetic field variations as part of the IMAGE high-latitude magnetometer network, supporting ionospheric, magnetospheric, and auroral studies; it has no orbital phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Kenai: Kenai Geophysical Observatory is a ground geomagnetic station at Kenai, Alaska, in the USGS geomagnetic observatory network; it has no orbit or changing vantage point. Its operational start year/end status are not confirmed here. The station’s magnetometer measures local geomagnetic-field variations for ionospheric, magnetospheric, auroral-current, and space-weather studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/DMSP_5D-3/F18: DMSP 5D-3/F18 is a U.S. Defense Meteorological Satellite Program spacecraft launched in 2009 and operating in a near-circular, Sun-synchronous polar low-Earth orbit at about 830–850 km; its orbital class has not changed. It monitors space weather and the upper atmosphere/ionosphere, including auroral particle precipitation, thermal plasma, magnetic fields, and environmental imagery.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/GOES/12: NOAA’s GOES-12 (launched 2001; operational 2003-2013) was a geostationary weather/space-weather satellite carrying a triaxial fluxgate magnetometer for in-situ geomagnetic field vectors. It served as GOES-East near 75°W from 2003 to April 2010, then was relocated near 60°W for South America coverage until retirement in 2013.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/NOAA/16: NOAA-16 (launched 2000, operated until 2014) was a POES satellite in a near-circular, Sun-synchronous polar low-Earth orbit (~850 km, ~99° inclination) throughout its mission. It carried SEM-2 instruments including MEPED and TED to measure trapped and precipitating energetic electrons/protons and auroral particles for space weather, radiation belt, and auroral studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/DSCOVR: DSCOVR (Deep Space Climate Observatory, launched 2015) is a NOAA/NASA/USAF mission in a halo/Lissajous orbit about the Sun-Earth L1 point from mid-2015 onward; its orbit has not changed. For heliophysics it provides upstream solar wind plasma and interplanetary magnetic-field measurements for space-weather monitoring and studies, using the PlasMag instrument suite.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Voyager2: NASA’s Voyager 2 (launched 1977) is a planetary and heliospheric probe on a heliocentric escape trajectory. It flew by Jupiter in 1979, Saturn in 1981, Uranus in 1986, and Neptune in 1989, measuring planetary magnetospheres, plasma, fields, particles, and waves; afterward it explored the outer heliosphere, crossed the termination shock in 2007 and the heliopause in 2018, and now samples the very local interstellar medium.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/SAMPEX: SAMPEX (Solar, Anomalous, and Magnetospheric Particle Explorer, 1992-2012) flew a single decaying near-polar low-Earth orbit, initially about 520 x 670 km at 82° inclination, until atmospheric reentry. It measured energetic ions and electrons in near-Earth space, including anomalous cosmic rays, solar energetic particles, trapped radiation-belt and magnetospheric populations, using instruments such as HILT, MAST, PET, and LICA.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/3G: BARREL-3G was an individual NASA BARREL stratospheric balloon payload operated in 2015 during the third long-duration balloon campaign from Esrange/Kiruna, Sweden, drifting at float altitude across the Arctic rather than orbiting. It measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from precipitating radiation-belt electrons, with GPS ephemeris and magnetic-field data.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Sakigake: Sakigake (MS-T5) was Japan/ISAS’s first deep-space probe (launched 1985; contact lost 1995), measuring interplanetary magnetic fields, solar-wind plasma waves, and energetic particles. It flew in heliocentric orbit after launch, passed Comet Halley in March 1986, then made an Earth gravity-assist flyby in January 1992 and continued on a revised heliocentric trajectory.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/3B: BARREL-3B was a NASA/Dartmouth long-duration balloon payload in the BARREL program, launched for the 2013-2014 Antarctic campaign and ending after that single flight. It flew in the high-latitude stratosphere over Antarctica on circumpolar winds, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays from precipitating radiation-belt electrons, with GPS/ephemeris and magnetic-field context for geospace studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/2C: BARREL-2C was a NASA/Dartmouth BARREL balloon payload operated during the second Antarctic campaign in the 2013-2014 austral season, ending in 2014. It was not in space orbit; it drifted in the Antarctic stratosphere with circumpolar winds, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation plus magnetic field and GPS ephemeris for magnetospheric space-weather studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/3C: BARREL-3C was a Dartmouth/NASA BARREL stratospheric balloon payload, launched and operated in 2015 during the third BARREL campaign from Esrange/Kiruna, Sweden, flying at high altitude over northern high-latitude regions until flight termination that year. It measured bremsstrahlung X-rays/gamma rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, with magnetometer and GPS context.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Kaktovik: The Kaktovik Geophysical Observatory is a fixed Arctic ground station at Kaktovik/Barter Island on Alaska’s North Slope, operating at least by 1995 with no known end date. Its fluxgate magnetometer records local geomagnetic-field variations at auroral latitudes for studies of ionospheric currents, magnetospheric disturbances, substorms, and space weather.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/TWINS1: TWINS-1, a NASA mission-of-opportunity payload launched in 2006 on the USA-184/NROL-22 spacecraft, operated for heliophysics science from 2008 to 2020. Its orbit did not change: a 12-hour, highly elliptical Molniya-type Earth orbit at about 63° inclination, giving high-latitude apogee views of the magnetosphere. It used wide-angle energetic neutral atom imagers and Lyman-alpha sensors to study the ring current, geocorona, and global magnetospheric dynamics.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Richards: Richardson Geophysical Observatory is a ground-based magnetometer site in Richardson, Alaska; its exact operational start/end are not clear from SPASE/CDAWeb metadata. It measures local geomagnetic field variations for ionospheric, magnetospheric, auroral, and space-weather studies, providing fixed high-latitude ground magnetic observations rather than any orbital vantage point.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Kiana: Kiana Geophysical Observatory is a ground magnetometer station at Kiana, Alaska, used in high-latitude magnetic monitoring networks. Operational since at least the 1990s, it measures local geomagnetic field variations for auroral ionosphere, magnetosphere, substorm, and current-system studies; as a fixed ground site it has no orbital phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/OMNI: OMNI is a NASA virtual observatory/data set, not a spacecraft, providing near-Earth solar wind and IMF observations from 1963 to present. It combines and intercalibrates measurements from many upstream/near-Earth spacecraft, including IMP, ISEE, Wind, ACE, and DSCOVR, and time-shifts them to Earth’s bow-shock nose for heliospheric and geospace studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Hawkeye: Hawkeye 1 (launched 1974, operated until 1978) was a University of Iowa/NASA heliophysics spacecraft in a highly elliptical near-polar Earth orbit, about 465 km perigee and 125,000 km apogee, not a low-altitude-only orbit. It measured high-latitude magnetospheric and ionospheric electrodynamics, auroral currents, magnetic fields, plasma waves/VLF emissions, and particle-related phenomena.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Upernavi: Upernavik Geophysical Observatory (UPN), a fixed ground station at Upernavik, northwest Greenland (~72.8°N, 56.1°W), has operated since at least the early 1980s as part of Greenland/high-latitude magnetometer networks. It records local geomagnetic field variations for auroral electrojet, ionospheric current, and magnetospheric disturbance studies; no orbital phases apply.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/2O: BARREL-2O was a NASA/Dartmouth BARREL stratospheric balloon payload flown during the second Antarctic campaign in 2013-2014, drifting in the Antarctic polar vortex at ~30-40 km altitude rather than orbiting Earth. It measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from precipitating radiation-belt electrons, with magnetic and GPS/trajectory context, to study radiation-belt loss.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Fort.Yat: Fort Yates Geophysical Observatory is a ground magnetometer station at Fort Yates, North Dakota, USA, used for geomagnetic-field variation observations relevant to ionospheric and magnetospheric current systems and space-weather studies; it has no orbit or spacecraft phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Longyear: The Longyearbyen Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground magnetometer station at Longyearbyen, Svalbard (78.2°N, 15.8°E), operational by 1991 in the IMAGE magnetometer network and used in CDAWeb. It measures high-latitude geomagnetic field variations, auroral electrojets, and cusp/polar-cap current systems; its location/vantage point does not change.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Nyalesun: Ny-Ålesund (NAL) is a fixed ground geomagnetic observatory at Ny-Ålesund, Svalbard, Norway, operational in space-physics archives from at least 1993 and continuing. Its magnetometer records local high-latitude geomagnetic field variations near cusp/polar-cap footprints for studies of ionospheric currents, substorms, and magnetospheric disturbances.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/ELFIN/B: ELFIN-B (Electron Losses and Fields Investigation B) was a UCLA/NASA 3U CubeSat launched in 2018 and operated until its 2022 decay/reentry in a single low-Earth, near-polar orbit with no major orbit changes beyond atmospheric decay. It measured radiation-belt electron and ion precipitation, pitch-angle distributions, and magnetic fields to study wave-particle loss into the atmosphere.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/2X: BARREL-2X was an individual NASA Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses payload flown on an Antarctic long-duration balloon during the second BARREL campaign in austral summer 2013-2014. From the stratosphere over/around Antarctica, it measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from precipitating radiation-belt electrons, magnetic field, and GPS position; it had no space orbit.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/TWINS2: TWINS-2 (launched 2008 on a U.S. national-security host satellite) is a NASA Explorer Mission of Opportunity for magnetospheric remote sensing. It has remained in a 12-hour, high-inclination Molniya-type highly elliptical Earth orbit, imaging Earth’s ring current and magnetosphere with energetic neutral atom spectrometers and measuring geocoronal/interplanetary neutral H via a Lyman-alpha detector.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Suisei: Suisei (PLANET-A) was an ISAS/Japan comet and solar-wind probe (launched 1985; operations ended 1992). It entered a low-inclination heliocentric orbit, imaged Comet Halley’s H I Lyman-alpha coma and measured solar-wind plasma, made a close Halley flyby on 8 Mar 1986 (~151,000 km), then continued heliocentric cruise with trajectory corrections toward an Earth-return flyby in Aug 1992.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Genesis: NASA’s Genesis mission (2001-2004) studied solar wind composition and returned collected ions to Earth. After launch it transferred to the Sun-Earth L1 region, operating in a halo orbit there from late 2001 to April 2004; it then departed L1 for an Earth-return trajectory, releasing its sample capsule in September 2004. GIM and GEM measured solar wind ions and electrons.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/2W: BARREL-2W was a NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses payload flown in the 2013-2014 Antarctic campaign. It was a stratospheric balloon over Antarctica, not an orbiting spacecraft, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays from precipitating radiation-belt electrons and magnetic perturbations to study wave-particle interactions.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BepiColombo: ESA-JAXA’s BepiColombo (launched 2018) is a dual-spacecraft Mercury/heliophysics mission. During its 2018-2026 cruise it traverses the inner heliosphere using Earth, Venus, and multiple Mercury flybys, making solar-wind and planetary encounter measurements. After Mercury orbit insertion planned in 2026, ESA’s MPO and JAXA’s Mio will study Mercury, its magnetic field, magnetosphere, exosphere, surface, and solar-wind interaction.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/ST5-155: ST5-155 was one of NASA’s three Space Technology 5 microsatellites, launched in 2006 and operated until mid-2006. It flew a highly elliptical, high-inclination low-Earth orbit, roughly 300–4500 km altitude at about 105.6° inclination, with no major orbital relocation. ST5 demonstrated miniature spacecraft technologies and measured Earth’s magnetic field for magnetospheric/space-weather studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/2M: BARREL-2M was a NASA/Dartmouth BARREL high-altitude balloon payload operated in the 2013-2014 Antarctic campaign, drifting in the stratospheric polar vortex over Antarctica rather than orbiting Earth. It measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from precipitating radiation-belt electrons, with magnetometer and GPS data, to study electron loss and magnetosphere–ionosphere coupling.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/SESAME: SESAME (operational from 1988, with archived campaigns mainly in the late 1980s–1990s) was a Scandinavian auroral-zone ground observatory network in northern Fennoscandia, not a spacecraft. It measured ionospheric and magnetospheric variability using riometers, VLF/ELF receivers, all-sky imagers, Fabry–Perot interferometers, and magnetometers for auroral and space-weather studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/2P: BARREL-2P was a NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for RBSP Relativistic Electron Losses payload, flown as a long-duration stratospheric balloon over Antarctica during the second BARREL campaign in 2014, ending the same year. It supported Van Allen Probes radiation-belt studies by measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays from precipitating energetic electrons, with magnetometer and position data.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Galileo: NASA's Galileo spacecraft (launched 1989, ended 2003) measured magnetic fields, plasma, energetic particles, dust, and radio/plasma waves for Jupiter-system science. It followed a Venus-Earth-Earth gravity-assist cruise in 1989-95, with Venus, Earth, Gaspra, and Ida encounters and interplanetary measurements, then orbited Jupiter in highly elliptical moon-crossing orbits from Dec 1995 until Jupiter impact in Sep 2003.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Pioneer11: NASA’s Pioneer 11 (launched 1973; last contact/mission end 1995) was a deep-space heliophysics and planetary probe. It cruised heliocentrically to Jupiter in 1973-74, flew through Jupiter’s magnetosphere in Dec 1974, traveled onward to Saturn in 1974-79, flew by Saturn in Sep 1979, then continued on a heliocentric escape trajectory measuring solar wind, magnetic fields, plasma, energetic particles, and cosmic rays.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/1O: BARREL-1O was a NASA/Dartmouth stratospheric balloon payload flown during the first BARREL Antarctic campaign in 2013 (ended 2013), launched from Antarctica and drifting at roughly 30–40 km altitude over Antarctica/Southern Ocean rather than orbiting. It measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from precipitating radiation-belt electrons, with magnetic-field and GPS/ephemeris data.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Cassini: NASA/ESA/ASI Cassini (launched 1997, ended 2017) studied Saturn’s system and fields/particles. It cruised heliocentrically with gravity assists at Venus (1998, 1999), Earth (1999), and Jupiter (2000, with Jovian magnetosphere science), then entered Saturn orbit in 2004 for tour/extended missions through 2017, including 2017 ring-grazing/Grand Finale proximal orbits. MAG measured in-situ magnetic fields in the solar wind and planetary magnetospheres.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Apollo12-LM: Apollo 12 Lunar Module/ALSEP (launched and deployed in November 1969; ALSEP operated until September 1977) was not an orbital spacecraft but a fixed lunar-surface station at the Oceanus Procellarum landing site. It measured the local lunar plasma, magnetic, seismic, and thermal environment; the Solar Wind Spectrometer and related plasma instruments observed solar wind ions/electrons from the Moon.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/2B: BARREL-2B was a NASA Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses payload launched in the 2013-2014 Antarctic campaign and ended in 2014. It flew as a long-duration stratospheric balloon over Antarctica, drifting in the polar vortex at about 30-40 km altitude, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays from precipitating radiation-belt electrons and local magnetic fields.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/NOAA/5: NOAA-5 was a NOAA polar-orbiting environmental satellite launched in 1976 and operated until 1979. It remained in a near-polar, Sun-synchronous low-Earth orbit throughout its mission, with no distinct relocation phases. Its Solar Proton Monitor measured energetic proton and alpha-particle fluxes for space-weather and near-Earth particle-environment studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Mekrijar: Mekrijärvi Geophysical Observatory is a ground geomagnetic station at Ilomantsi, eastern Finland, operating since at least the early 1990s in the IMAGE magnetometer network. It measures local geomagnetic field variations for auroral electrojet, ionospheric current, magnetic-pulsation, and magnetospheric studies; it has no orbital phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Cluster/C4: Cluster-C4 (Tango), launched in 2000 and operated for science to 2024, was one of ESA’s four Cluster spacecraft. It remained in an evolving highly elliptical, near-polar Earth orbit throughout, initially about 4 x 19.6 Earth radii with a 57-hour period, with changing separations/local times sampling the bow shock, magnetosheath, magnetopause, cusps, magnetotail, plasmasphere, and auroral regions using plasma, field, energetic-particle, and wave instruments.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/1Q: BARREL-1Q was a BARREL long-duration stratospheric balloon payload flown over Antarctica in early 2013, drifting in the polar vortex at about 30–40 km altitude. It measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from precipitating radiation-belt electrons, with magnetometer and GPS context, for magnetospheric space-weather studies coordinated with the Van Allen Probes.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/4H: BARREL-4H was a NASA/Dartmouth high-altitude Antarctic balloon payload in the BARREL radiation-belt campaign, operating during its 2016 flight over Antarctica. It drifted with polar stratospheric winds, carrying an X-ray spectrometer to measure bremsstrahlung from precipitating radiation-belt electrons and support Van Allen Probes magnetospheric loss studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/LANL/1989: LANL-1989 (launched 1989, operated to 2007) was a Los Alamos National Laboratory geosynchronous Earth-orbit spacecraft for magnetospheric and space-weather research. It stayed at/near GEO throughout its mission, sampling the near-Earth plasma sheet/ring-current region; MPA measured 3D ions/electrons and SOPA measured energetic particles.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Equator-S: Equator-S was a German-led magnetospheric spacecraft launched in 1997 and operated until 1998. It flew a fixed, highly elliptical, low-inclination near-equatorial Earth orbit, about 500 km perigee to 67,000 km apogee, to study the dayside magnetosphere, magnetopause, and equatorial boundary regions using magnetic/electric fields, plasma, energetic-particle, and wave measurements.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Park.Sit: Park Site Geophysical Observatory is a ground magnetometer site at Park Site, Antarctica; its operational start and end years are not confidently documented in the provided registry context. It records geomagnetic field variations for studies of high-latitude ionospheric currents, auroral electrodynamics, and magnetospheric disturbances.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/IMP8: IMP-8 (Explorer 50; 1973-2001) was a NASA interplanetary monitor in a high-altitude geocentric orbit, often described as nearly circular at about 35 Earth radii with a ~12.5-day period, repeatedly sampling the upstream solar wind, bow shock/magnetosheath, and distant magnetotail. It measured magnetic fields, plasma, energetic particles, and cosmic rays for heliospheric and magnetospheric studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Remus: Remus Geophysical Observatory is a ground magnetometer station at Remus, Michigan, USA, with CDAWeb records beginning around 2006 and no orbit or relocation. It measures local geomagnetic field vector variations for studies of magnetic storms, substorms, ULF waves, and space-weather coupling to Earth’s magnetosphere and ionosphere.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/NOAA/6: NOAA-6 was a NOAA polar-orbiting environmental satellite (launched 1979, operated until 1987) in a near-circular Sun-synchronous low Earth polar orbit at roughly 800–850 km altitude and ~99° inclination; its orbit did not have distinct science phases. Its Space Environment Monitor measured trapped and precipitating energetic electrons and protons for magnetospheric, radiation-belt, and space-weather studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/1H: BARREL-1H was a NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses stratospheric balloon payload, operated during the 2013 Antarctic long-duration balloon campaign. It drifted at ~30–40 km over Antarctica and the Southern Ocean, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays/gamma rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation with GPS and geospace context data.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/ICON: NASA’s ICON (Ionospheric Connection Explorer; launched 2019) studied ionosphere-thermosphere coupling from a low-inclination (~27°), ~575 km low-Earth orbit that did not undergo major mission-phase changes. Science operations ran from late 2019 until contact was lost in Nov 2022 (mission formally ended 2024), using MIGHTI, FUV, EUV, and IVM for winds, airglow/UV emissions, and in situ plasma.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/1A: BARREL-1A was a NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses payload flown on a long-duration stratospheric balloon over Antarctica during the early-2013 campaign. It drifted with the polar vortex at about 35–40 km rather than orbiting Earth, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation and local magnetic fields in conjunction with Van Allen Probes.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/4E: BARREL-4E was a NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses payload, operating as a long-duration high-altitude balloon over Antarctica during the 2016 BARREL campaign. It measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from precipitating radiation-belt electrons for magnetospheric loss and space-weather studies, in conjunction with spacecraft such as the Van Allen Probes.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/SuperDARN: SuperDARN (Super Dual Auroral Radar Network) is an international ground-based HF coherent-scatter radar network, begun with Goose Bay in 1983 and organized/expanded as SuperDARN from 1995, with high- and mid-latitude radars in both hemispheres. It measures ionospheric plasma convection, electric fields, and decameter irregularities for magnetosphere–ionosphere coupling and space-weather studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Lyford: Lyford Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground-based geomagnetic station at Lyford, Texas, USA, measuring local magnetic-field variations with a magnetometer for ionospheric, magnetospheric, and space-weather studies; it has no orbital phases or relocations. Operational start/end years are not confidently confirmed in available metadata.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Dead.Hor: Dead Horse Geophysical Observatory (operational by 2006 in CDAWeb/THEMIS-era holdings) is a fixed ground magnetometer station at Deadhorse/Prudhoe Bay, Alaska, not a spacecraft. It measures local vector geomagnetic field variations for auroral-zone, high-latitude ionosphere-magnetosphere, and space-weather studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/2E: BARREL-2E was a NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for RBSP Relativistic Electron Losses payload, launched and operated only during its 2014 Antarctic long-duration stratospheric balloon flight. Drifting over Antarctica rather than orbiting, it measured bremsstrahlung X rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, with magnetic-field, GPS, and housekeeping data for conjunctions with the Van Allen Probes.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/SNOE: Student Nitric Oxide Explorer (SNOE, 1998-2003) was a small NASA/STEDI low-Earth-orbit satellite in a near-circular, near-polar Sun-synchronous orbit about 535-580 km altitude until orbital decay/reentry. It studied the lower thermosphere and ionosphere, measuring nitric oxide ultraviolet airglow, solar soft X-rays, and auroral electrons/photons driving space-weather variability.
spase://NASA/Observatory/AeroCube-6/A: AeroCube-6A (AC6-A), launched in 2014 and operated for science through 2017, was a CubeSat radiation-belt mission in near-polar low Earth orbit (~620–700 km altitude, ~98° inclination), with no major orbital-phase changes beyond orbital decay. It measured energetic electron/proton fluxes with a dosimeter to study radiation-belt precipitation and microbursts.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Cape.Dor: Cape Dorset Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground geomagnetic station at Cape Dorset/Kinngait, Nunavut, Canada, in operation since at least the early 1980s. It measures local geomagnetic field variations with magnetometers for ionospheric, magnetospheric, auroral-zone, and space-weather studies; it has no orbital phases or changing vantage point.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Athabasc: Athabasca Geophysical Observatory is a ground station at Athabasca, Alberta, Canada, used in heliophysics observations from at least the THEMIS ground-based era (2006 onward). It has no orbit; it records local geomagnetic field variations with a fluxgate magnetometer for ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/ST5-224: ST5-224 was one of NASA’s three Space Technology 5 microsatellites, launched and operated in 2006 until mission end later that year. It flew a highly elliptical, near-polar low-Earth orbit, with no major orbital relocation, demonstrating nanosatellite constellation technologies while its miniature fluxgate magnetometer measured Earth’s magnetic field, auroral currents, and magnetospheric structure.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Scheffer: Schefferville Geophysical Observatory is a ground geophysical/magnetic station at Schefferville, Quebec, Canada, operational from the IGY era (about 1957) in high-latitude North America. It measures geomagnetic field variations with ground magnetometers for ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies; as a fixed ground site it has no orbital phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/AMPTE-CCE: AMPTE-CCE (Charge Composition Explorer), launched in 1984 and operated until 1989, was one of the three AMPTE spacecraft. It remained in a near-equatorial, highly elliptical Earth orbit (about 1,100–50,000 km altitude) throughout the mission, sampling the inner magnetosphere, ring current, and radiation belts with energetic-particle, ion-composition, plasma, and fields measurements.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Fort.Chu: Fort Churchill Geophysical Observatory (established for the IGY in 1957) is a ground geophysical/magnetic station at or near Churchill, Manitoba, Canada, not a spacecraft. It measures local geomagnetic field variations with magnetometers for auroral-zone ionospheric currents, substorms, and geomagnetic-storm studies; CDAWeb holdings may represent only specific instrument campaigns.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Toolik.L: Toolik Lake Geophysical Observatory (operational since at least the mid-1990s) is a fixed ground magnetometer station at Toolik Lake, Alaska, measuring geomagnetic field variations for high-latitude ionospheric and magnetospheric studies, including auroral currents, substorms, and ULF pulsations; its observing location does not change.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/4C: BARREL-4C was one Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses payload, operated in 2016 as a high-altitude stratospheric balloon in the northern polar campaign launched from Esrange/Kiruna, Sweden, not a spacecraft orbit. It measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, with GPS ephemeris and housekeeping, for magnetospheric space-weather studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Bay.Mill: Bay Mills Geophysical Observatory is a ground magnetic station at Bay Mills, Michigan, USA, used for heliophysics and space-weather studies of geomagnetic and ionospheric current systems. It has no orbit; it measures local geomagnetic field variations with a magnetometer. Exact operational start/end years are not confirmed in the supplied SPASE/CDAWeb summary.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Hot.Spri: Hot Springs Geophysical Observatory is a ground magnetic observatory at Hot Springs, South Dakota, USA, operational from at least 1960 in available geomagnetic records. It uses ground magnetometers to measure local geomagnetic-field variations for studies of magnetic storms, ionospheric currents, and secular/space-weather geomagnetic activity; it has no orbital phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/2A: BARREL-2A was a NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses payload launched over Antarctica in December 2013 and operated into January 2014. It was a long-duration stratospheric balloon, not an orbital spacecraft, drifting over Antarctica to measure bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, with magnetic field, GPS, and engineering data.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Juno: NASA’s Juno spacecraft (launched 2011) studies Jupiter’s interior, gravity/magnetic fields, aurorae, plasma, energetic particles, and radio/plasma waves. It cruised in heliocentric orbit from 2011-2016, including an Oct. 2013 Earth gravity assist, then entered a highly elliptical polar Jovian orbit in July 2016; its extended mission from 2021 used the evolving orbit for close Ganymede, Europa, and Io flybys while sampling Jupiter’s magnetosphere.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Pinawa: Pinawa Geophysical Observatory (PIN), operating in Pinawa, Manitoba, Canada since 1968, is a ground magnetic observatory measuring geomagnetic field variations with magnetometers for ionospheric, magnetospheric, and space-weather studies; it contributes data to INTERMAGNET/CANMOS and CDAWeb.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Interball-2: Interball-2 (Auroral Probe, launched 1996; science operations ended 1998) studied Earth’s auroral magnetosphere and ionosphere from a single highly elliptical, high-inclination Earth orbit, about 700–20,000 km altitude at ~63° inclination. It sampled auroral zones, polar cusp, and magnetospheric boundaries, measuring plasma, energetic particles, electric and magnetic fields, and waves.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Fort.Nel: Fort Nelson Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground-based geomagnetic station at Fort Nelson, British Columbia, Canada, operating since at least the CDAWeb data era to measure local magnetic-field variations for ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies; it has no orbital phases or changing space vantage point.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Geotail: Geotail (JAXA/NASA, 1992-2022) studied Earth’s magnetotail, magnetosphere, bow shock, and solar wind with plasma, particle, electric- and magnetic-field instruments. From 1992 to late 1994 it used lunar swingbys to sample the distant magnetotail, reaching roughly 80-220 Earth radii downtail; from 1995 onward it remained in a lower highly elliptical geocentric orbit sampling the near-tail and dayside boundary regions.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Magion-4: Magion-4 was a Czech microsatellite of the Interball Tail Probe mission, launched in 1995 and operated until 1997. It flew the same highly elliptical geocentric magnetotail orbit throughout its life, with apogee near 200,000 km and perigee a few hundred km, sampling the magnetosphere, bow shock, magnetosheath, auroral/plasma regions, fields, waves, and energetic particles.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/THEMIS/D: THEMIS-D (launched 2007) is one of NASA’s THEMIS probes studying terrestrial substorms, magnetotail dynamics, plasma, fields, and energetic particles. After commissioning and orbit raising in 2007 it has remained a near-equatorial, highly elliptical Earth orbiting inner THEMIS probe, with roughly 1-day geocentric orbits and apogee near the magnetosphere/magnetotail; it did not transfer to lunar ARTEMIS orbit.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/3F: BARREL-3F was a NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses stratospheric balloon payload, launched and ended in 2015 during BARREL’s third campaign, apparently from Esrange/Kiruna, Sweden, drifting at stratospheric altitude over Arctic longitudes rather than orbiting. It measured X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, magnetic field, and ephemeris/housekeeping data.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/MetOp/A: MetOp-A was a EUMETSAT/ESA polar-orbiting meteorological satellite launched in 2006 and retired in 2021. During its science operations it flew a near-polar, Sun-synchronous low Earth orbit at about 817 km altitude with a mid-morning local time node; it was lowered/passivated for disposal in 2021. Its SEM-2 instrument measured energetic electrons, protons, and radiation-belt particle fluxes for space-weather and near-Earth magnetospheric studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/NOAA/14: NOAA-14 (NOAA-J, launched 1994; operational environmental service to 2005) was a NOAA polar-orbiting weather satellite in a near-polar, sun-synchronous low Earth orbit for its mission, with no major relocation. Its Space Environment Monitor measured energetic protons and electrons in near-Earth radiation belts and auroral/precipitating particle regions for magnetospheric and space-weather studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/NOAA/18: NOAA-18 (NOAA-N), launched in 2005 and operational until 2025, was a NOAA POES satellite in a near-polar Sun-synchronous low Earth orbit throughout its mission. Its SEM-2 package measured precipitating and trapped energetic particles, auroral electrons/protons, and radiation-belt populations for space weather and geospace studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Soroya: Sørøya Geophysical Observatory (SOR) is a fixed ground magnetic observatory on Sørøya, northern Norway, in operation by at least the CDAWeb data era; it has no orbital phases. It records geomagnetic field variations with magnetometers for auroral-zone ionospheric, magnetospheric, and geomagnetic-disturbance studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Nuuk: Nuuk Geophysical Observatory (Godthåb/GHB or NUK), operating since about 1976, is a ground geomagnetic station at Nuuk, Greenland, in the Greenland magnetometer network. It measures local vector geomagnetic-field variations for auroral, ionospheric, and magnetospheric studies; as a fixed ground observatory it has no orbital phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Kilpisja: Kilpisjärvi Geophysical Observatory (operational since about 1981) is a fixed ground observatory at Kilpisjärvi in Finnish Lapland, in the auroral zone. It supports heliophysics and space-weather studies with all-sky auroral optical imaging and geomagnetic field variation measurements; its KIL magnetometer station is part of the IMAGE network.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/The.Pas: The Pas is a fixed ground-based magnetometer station at The Pas, Manitoba, Canada, operating by the Canadian CANOPUS/CDAWeb era in the late 1980s. It measures local geomagnetic field variations for ionospheric and magnetospheric studies, including auroral electrojets, substorms, ULF waves, and geomagnetic disturbances.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Donna: Donna Geophysical Observatory is a ground-based geomagnetic observatory at Donna, Texas, USA, operating magnetometers to record local geomagnetic field variations for ionospheric, magnetospheric, and geomagnetic studies; it has no orbital phases. Its exact operational start/end dates for CDAWeb/SPASE use are not confirmed here.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/PioneerVenusOrb: NASA’s Pioneer Venus Orbiter (Pioneer 12; launched 1978, operated at Venus 1978–1992) studied Venus’s atmosphere, ionosphere, induced magnetosphere, and solar-wind interaction. It remained in a highly elliptical, near-polar ~24-h Venus orbit, with low-periapsis aeronomy passes and distant apoapsis/wake sampling, until atmospheric entry in 1992.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Nordkapp: Nordkapp Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground-based magnetometer station at Nordkapp, Norway, measuring local geomagnetic-field variations for high-latitude ionospheric, auroral-electrojet, and magnetospheric studies; no spacecraft orbit applies. Operational start/end are not confidently specified here.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Linares: Linares Geophysical Observatory is a ground geomagnetic station at Linares, Chile, with records reported from at least the IGY era (1957 onward, end date not confirmed). It measures geomagnetic field variations with magnetometers for studies of Earth’s magnetic field, ionospheric/magnetospheric currents, geomagnetic storms, and space weather; it has no orbital phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/IBEX: IBEX (Interstellar Boundary Explorer), launched in 2008, is a NASA heliophysics mission using IBEX-Lo and IBEX-Hi energetic-neutral-atom imagers to map the heliosphere’s outer boundary and solar-wind interaction with the local interstellar medium. It has remained in Earth orbit: 2008-2011 in a very high, highly elliptical orbit, then from 2011 in a more stable lunar-resonant high elliptical geocentric orbit.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/CNOFS: C/NOFS (Communication/Navigation Outage Forecasting System) was a USAF/NASA equatorial ionosphere mission launched in 2008 and operated until reentry in 2015. It remained in a low-inclination (~13°), elliptical low-Earth orbit (initially about 400 x 850 km, gradually decaying), measuring plasma density/composition, ion drifts, neutral winds, electric fields, and scintillation-related irregularities.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Tasiilaq: Tasiilaq Geophysical Observatory is a ground geophysical/magnetic station in Tasiilaq, southeast Greenland, operated as part of Greenland geomagnetic monitoring and contributing data to CDAWeb. It measures local geomagnetic field variations for ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies; it is a fixed ground site, not an orbiting mission. Operational start is not confidently verified here.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Helios1: Helios 1 (Helios-A) was a German/NASA solar probe launched in 1974; it returned inner-heliosphere science data mainly until 1982. Its vantage point did not change: it remained in a highly eccentric heliocentric near-ecliptic orbit of about 0.31-0.98 AU, period ~190 days, measuring solar-wind plasma, magnetic fields, energetic particles, cosmic rays, dust, and radio/plasma waves.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/San.Anto: San Antonio Geophysical Observatory was a fixed ground-based geomagnetic/magnetometer station in San Antonio, Texas, with CDAWeb holdings from at least the International Geophysical Year era (1957; exact start/end not clear in registry metadata). It recorded local geomagnetic-field variations for magnetospheric, ionospheric, geomagnetic-storm, and space-weather studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Nain: Nain Geophysical Observatory (operational by at least the 1980s; exact start/end not confirmed) is a fixed ground magnetometer/geophysical station at Nain, Labrador, Canada, measuring local geomagnetic field variations for ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies in high-latitude monitoring networks; it has no orbital phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Maniitso: Maniitsoq Geophysical Observatory has operated at Maniitsoq, formerly Sukkertoppen, on Greenland’s west coast since about 1972–1973; it is a fixed ground station with no orbit. It records local geomagnetic field variations with ground magnetometers for auroral electrojet, ionospheric current, magnetic storm, and magnetospheric studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Homer: Homer Geophysical Observatory (HOM) is a fixed ground magnetometer station at Homer, Alaska, USA (about 59.6°N, 151.6°W). Documented in CDAWeb-era archives from 1978, it measures local geomagnetic-field variations for auroral, ionospheric, and magnetospheric current/substorm studies; as a ground site it has no orbital phases or changing vantage point.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/NOAA/7: NOAA-7 (launched 1981; operated until 1986) was a NOAA TIROS-N-series polar weather satellite in low-Earth, near-polar Sun-synchronous orbit, with no major orbital phase changes. Its Space Environment Monitor measured energetic electron and proton fluxes, including trapped and precipitating particles, for radiation-belt, auroral, and space-weather studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Voyager1: NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft (launched 1977; operating) is a planetary/heliospheric probe. It flew by Jupiter in March 1979 and Saturn/Titan in November 1980 with fields, particles, plasma-wave, and remote-sensing observations, then followed a solar-system escape heliocentric trajectory north of the ecliptic. It crossed the termination shock in 2004 and heliopause in 2012, measuring energetic particles, magnetic fields, and plasma waves in the outer heliosphere and local interstellar medium.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Qeqertar: Qeqertarsuaq Geophysical Observatory, formerly Godhavn/GDH, is a ground geomagnetic station at Qeqertarsuaq on Disko Island, Greenland, where magnetic observations began in 1926 and continue today. It has no orbit; its magnetometers measure local geomagnetic-field variations for auroral electrojet, ionospheric current, and magnetospheric disturbance studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/ELFIN/A: ELFIN-A (Electron Losses and Fields Investigation; launched 2018) is a UCLA 3U CubeSat in near-polar low Earth orbit, initially about 450 km altitude and ~93° inclination, with no major orbit changes aside from natural orbital decay. It measures radiation-belt electron and ion pitch-angle distributions plus magnetic fields to study wave-particle scattering and atmospheric precipitation.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/DynamicsExplore: Dynamics Explorer 1 (DE 1, NASA Explorer 62; 1981-1991) flew a highly elliptical near-polar Earth orbit, about 570 x 23,000 km, sampling the magnetosphere, plasmasphere, auroral regions, and topside ionosphere. It measured fields, plasma waves, ion/electron populations, ion drift, neutral/auroral emissions, and global auroral images to study magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Danmarks: Danmarkshavn Geophysical Observatory (DMH), operating since 1948, is a fixed ground magnetic observatory at Danmarkshavn in northeast Greenland. It measures local geomagnetic field variations with fluxgate/absolute magnetometers and provides high-latitude magnetic data for geomagnetic monitoring, auroral electrojet studies, and global observatory networks; it has no orbital phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/WDC/San.Juan: San Juan WDC (IAGA code SJG) is a ground geomagnetic observatory in Puerto Rico, at/near San Juan and now near Cayey, operational since 1903. It measures local geomagnetic field variations with magnetometers, supporting studies of magnetic storms, Sq currents, and ionospheric/magnetospheric disturbances; data are distributed via the World Data Center/CDAWeb network.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/TIMED: TIMED (launched 2001) is a NASA heliophysics/upper-atmosphere mission in a near-circular low-Earth orbit, about 625 km altitude and 74° inclination; its orbit has had no major phase change. It studies the mesosphere, lower thermosphere, and ionosphere, measuring temperature, composition, winds, airglow, and solar EUV irradiance with instruments including SABER, GUVI, TIDI, and SEE.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Purcell: Purcell Geophysical Observatory is a ground-based geomagnetic station at Purcell, Oklahoma, USA; its operational start/end dates are not confirmed here. It operates a magnetometer measuring local geomagnetic field variations used for ionospheric, magnetospheric, geomagnetic-storm, and space-weather studies; as a fixed ground site, it has no orbital phases.
The Tristan da Cunha Geophysical Observatory is a ground geomagnetic station on Tristan da Cunha in the South Atlantic, operational by at least the mid-20th century, with no spacecraft orbit. It measures geomagnetic field variations using magnetometers for solar-terrestrial physics, geomagnetic disturbance, and space-weather studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Rosetta: ESA’s Rosetta spacecraft (launched 2004, ended 2016) studied comet 67P and its plasma, dust, gas, and nucleus. It cruised heliocentrically with Earth flybys in 2005/2007/2009, a Mars flyby in 2007, and asteroid flybys Šteins 2008 and Lutetia 2010; after 2011-14 hibernation it rendezvoused with 67P in Aug 2014, escorting it through perihelion until Sep 2016.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/THEMIS/Ground/C: THEMIS Ground CANMAG ATHA is the Athabasca, Alberta, Canada station of the THEMIS/Canadian ground magnetometer network, operational in CDAWeb from 2007 and continuing. It measures ground vector geomagnetic-field variations supporting studies of auroral currents, substorms, ULF waves, and magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling with THEMIS spacecraft.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/ISS: The International Space Station, assembled in low Earth orbit beginning in 1998 and continuously crewed since 2000, is a 51.6°-inclination platform at roughly 330-420 km altitude; its orbit is periodically reboosted but has not changed regime. It supports heliophysics and space-environment measurements of ionospheric plasma, radiation, cosmic rays, and spacecraft charging with instruments such as AMS-02, FPMU, and TEPC.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/McGrath: McGrath Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground magnetometer station at McGrath, Alaska, operational in CDAWeb at least in the THEMIS/ground-magnetometer era from the mid-2000s onward. It measures local geomagnetic field variations for studies of auroral-zone ionospheric currents, substorms, and magnetospheric dynamics; its vantage point does not change.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Inukjuak: Inukjuak Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground station at Inukjuak, Quebec, Canada, operational at least by the early 1990s and represented in CDAWeb for geomagnetic studies. It operates magnetometers measuring local geomagnetic field variations for auroral-ionospheric current and magnetospheric disturbance research as part of Canadian ground magnetic networks; it has no orbital or relocation phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Tartu: Tartu Geophysical Observatory is a ground magnetic observatory at Tõravere near Tartu, Estonia, operational since 1964 and still active. It has no orbit or changing vantage point; its magnetometers record local geomagnetic-field variations used for ionospheric, magnetospheric, geophysical, and space-weather studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Vize.Isl: Vize Island Geophysical Observatory (IAGA VIZ; operating since at least 1957) is a fixed ground geomagnetic station on Vize Island in the Russian high Arctic (~79.5°N, 77°E). It has no orbit or relocations; magnetometers record local vector/scalar magnetic-field variations for polar-cap electrodynamics, magnetic storms, and space-weather studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/MarsScienceLabo: NASA’s Mars Science Laboratory/Curiosity (launched 2011) cruised from Earth to Mars in 2011-2012, during which RAD measured interplanetary radiation and energetic particles. Since landing in Gale Crater in August 2012 it has operated as a Mars surface rover, measuring geology, atmosphere, climate, habitability, and the surface radiation environment; ephemerides give its changing traverse location on Mars.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Ekati: Ekati Geophysical Observatory (operational since about 1998) is a ground magnetic station at the Ekati diamond mine in Canada’s Northwest Territories. It measures geomagnetic field variations with fluxgate magnetometers for high-latitude magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling, auroral electrojet, and ionospheric current studies; its location/vantage point has not changed.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Jackvik: Jackvik Geophysical Observatory is a ground-based magnetometer station at Jäckvik/Jackvik, northern Sweden, in the auroral-zone Scandinavian network, recording local geomagnetic-field variations for ionospheric current, substorm, ULF-wave, and magnetospheric studies. It has no orbit or relocation phases; registry start/end dates are not confirmed.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Eagle: Eagle Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground magnetic observatory at Eagle, Alaska, active in USGS/CDAWeb geomagnetic records but with operational start/end dates not confirmed here. It measures local geomagnetic field variations, typically with fluxgate magnetometers, for ionospheric, magnetospheric, and space-weather studies; no orbital phases apply.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/FAST: FAST (Fast Auroral Snapshot Explorer) was a NASA SMEX mission launched in 1996 and operated until 2009 in a highly elliptical, near-polar low-Earth orbit (about 350 × 4175 km, 83° inclination) crossing the auroral zones. It measured auroral acceleration-region particles, electric and magnetic fields, plasma waves, and UV emissions for magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Ukiah: Ukiah Geophysical Observatory (UKI) was a fixed ground geomagnetic observatory at Ukiah, California, USA, operating roughly 1931/1932 to about 1983. It recorded local geomagnetic field variations with magnetometers/variometers for ionospheric, magnetospheric, and space-weather studies; as a ground site it had no orbital phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/NASA.Ste: NASA’s Stennis Space Center Geophysical Observatory (IAGA BSL) is a ground geomagnetic station at Stennis/Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, USA, operating since about 1986 and still active. It is not in orbit; it records local vector geomagnetic-field variations with fluxgate magnetometers for geophysics, magnetospheric studies, and space-weather monitoring.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Cluster/C2: ESA’s Cluster-C2/Salsa spacecraft (launched 2000; operated until atmospheric reentry in 2024) was one of four Cluster magnetospheric probes. Throughout the mission it flew an evolving, highly elliptical near-polar Earth orbit (about 4–19.6 RE initially, with natural/managed changes and variable tetrahedron separations), sampling magnetosphere, magnetotail, bow shock and solar wind with plasma, fields, energetic-particle and wave instruments.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/LANL/1997: LANL-1997 was a Los Alamos National Laboratory geosynchronous Earth-orbit spacecraft operating from 1997 to 2008. Its vantage point remained near geosynchronous orbit, where MPA and SOPA measured magnetospheric plasma and energetic electron/ion populations for radiation-belt, plasma sheet, and space-weather studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/NOAA/10: NOAA-10 was a NOAA POES/TIROS-N polar-orbiting environmental satellite (launched 1986; operational to 1991) in a near-circular Sun-synchronous low-Earth orbit at about 800–850 km and 98–99° inclination; its orbit did not have distinct science phases. Its SEM package measured precipitating/trapped energetic electrons and protons for radiation-belt, auroral, and space-weather studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/NOAA/12: NOAA-12 (launched 1991, decommissioned 2007) was a NOAA POES polar weather satellite that remained in low-Earth, near-polar Sun-synchronous orbit throughout its mission. For heliophysics it carried the Space Environment Monitor, including TED and MEPED sensors, measuring precipitating/trapped energetic electrons and protons in Earth’s radiation belts, auroral zones, and near-Earth space environment.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/NOAA/15: NOAA-15 (launched 1998; SEM-2 space-environment data commonly used through 2020) was a NOAA POES polar weather satellite in near-circular, near-polar Sun-synchronous low Earth orbit throughout its mission, with only normal local-time drift. Its SEM-2 package, including TED and MEPED, measured auroral particles, radiation-belt electrons/protons, and solar energetic particles.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/NOAA/19: NOAA-19 (NOAA-N Prime), launched in 2009, is a NOAA POES meteorological and space-weather satellite operating in near-polar, Sun-synchronous low Earth orbit at about 850 km; it has had no major orbital relocation beyond normal orbital/local-time drift. Its SEM-2 package measures energetic electrons and protons, auroral precipitation, radiation-belt particles, and solar proton events in near-Earth geospace.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Apollo15-LM: Apollo 15 Lunar Module/ALSEP (launched and deployed on the Moon in 1971; ALSEP operated until 1977) was a stationary lunar-surface observatory at the Hadley–Apennine landing site. It studied lunar geophysics and the near-surface plasma environment; the Solar Wind Spectrometer measured directional solar-wind proton and electron fluxes at the Moon.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Lethbrid: Lethbridge Geophysical Observatory (LTH; operating since 1986) is a ground magnetometer station at Lethbridge, Alberta, Canada, used in Canadian auroral/geospace networks including CANOPUS and successor CARISMA.
