It measures local geomagnetic field variations to study ionospheric currents, auroral activity, magnetic storms, ULF waves, and magnetospheric dynamics.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/ROCSAT-1: ROCSAT-1 (FORMOSAT-1), Taiwan’s first satellite, operated from 1999 to 2004 in a low-Earth, near-circular orbit about 600 km altitude at 35° inclination; its orbit did not have distinct science phases. It studied the low-latitude/topside ionosphere and equatorial plasma electrodynamics, with IPEI measuring ion density, composition, temperature, and drift.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Masi: Masi Geophysical Observatory (IMAGE station MAS) is a ground magnetic station at Masi, Norway, operating since at least the modern IMAGE/CDAWeb era to record geomagnetic field variations with a fluxgate magnetometer for auroral ionosphere and magnetosphere studies; it has no orbit or relocation, serving as a fixed high-latitude station in the IMAGE magnetometer network.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Prince.G: Prince George Geophysical Observatory (PGEO) is a fixed ground geophysical/magnetic observatory at Prince George, British Columbia, Canada, operational at least during the THEMIS/CDAWeb era beginning in 2007. It has no orbital phases; it measures local geomagnetic-field variations with a ground magnetometer for ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/NOAA/8: NOAA-8 was a NOAA polar-orbiting environmental satellite launched in 1983 and operated until 1985. It remained in a near-circular, Sun-synchronous, near-polar low Earth orbit throughout the mission, carrying the Space Environment Monitor (SEM) to measure precipitating/trapped energetic electrons and protons for space-weather, radiation-belt, and auroral studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/IGS: International GNSS Service (IGS, operational from 1994) is a global ground-based network of continuously operating GNSS/GPS receivers and analysis centers, not a spacecraft. It provides precise satellite tracking, orbit and clock products for geodesy and positioning, and heliophysics users derive global/regional ionospheric total electron content and scintillation-related diagnostics from its worldwide stations.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Roemoe: Roemoe is a ground geophysical observatory on Rømø, Denmark, measuring local geomagnetic field variations with a magnetometer for ionospheric, magnetospheric, and geomagnetic studies; it is fixed at this ground site, with no orbital phases. Its precise operational start/end years are not confirmed here, so use CDAWeb/SPASE metadata for dataset-specific coverage.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Saint.Fe: Saint-Félicien Geophysical Observatory is a ground geomagnetic station at Saint-Félicien, Quebec, Canada, operating at least during the CDAWeb-era records to measure local magnetic-field variations with ground magnetometers for ionospheric, magnetospheric, and geomagnetic-activity studies; as a fixed ground site it has no orbital phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Goose.Ba: Goose Bay Geophysical Observatory (operational by at least 1990; exact start/end not confirmed here) is a fixed ground magnetometer station at Goose Bay, Labrador, Canada, measuring geomagnetic field variations for auroral/subauroral current studies and regional/global geomagnetic monitoring; it has no orbital or relocation phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Akulivik: Akulivik Geophysical Observatory (operational by 2006; no end date reported) is a fixed ground station at Akulivik, Nunavik, Quebec, Canada, not a spacecraft. It records high-latitude geomagnetic field variations, chiefly with fluxgate magnetometers, for studies of auroral ionospheric currents, substorms, ULF waves, and magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling in Canadian/CDAWeb data products.
PENGUIn-1 is an Antarctic ground magnetometer station in the Polar Experiment Network for Geospace Upper-atmosphere Investigations, operational from about 2010 with CDAWeb records in the 2010s. It has no orbit; it measures local geomagnetic-field variations for studies of auroral electrodynamics, ionospheric and magnetospheric current systems, ULF waves, and space weather.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Kuujjuar: Kuujjuarapik Geophysical Observatory is a ground-based heliophysics station at Kuujjuarapik, Quebec, Canada (near 55.3°N, 77.8°W). Operational in CDAWeb/THEMIS ground-magnetometer records from 2006 onward, it has no orbit; it measures local three-component geomagnetic field variations for studies of auroral currents, ionospheric electrodynamics, substorms, and magnetospheric activity.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Daneborg: Daneborg Geophysical Observatory is a ground magnetic station at Daneborg in northeast Greenland, operational in space-physics data sets since at least the early 1980s and still active. It measures geomagnetic field variations with magnetometers for high-latitude ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies, and is included in the IMAGE/Greenland magnetometer networks.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Chibouga: Chibougamau Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground magnetic station at Chibougamau, Quebec, Canada, operational by at least the 1990s in CDAWeb/SPASE ground magnetometer records. It measures geomagnetic field variations for auroral, ionospheric, and magnetospheric studies; as a ground observatory it has no orbital or vantage-point changes.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Glyndon: Glyndon Geophysical Observatory is a ground-based magnetometer station near Glyndon, Minnesota, USA, operational no later than the CDAWeb archived data era; exact start and end dates are not confidently documented here. It measures local geomagnetic-field variations used for ionospheric, magnetospheric, ULF-wave, substorm, and space-weather studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Paamiut: Paamiut Geophysical Observatory is a ground station in Paamiut, southwest Greenland, operational since at least the CDAWeb data era and used for geomagnetic monitoring. It operates a magnetometer measuring local magnetic-field variations associated with ionospheric currents, auroral activity, and magnetospheric disturbances; as a fixed ground observatory, it has no orbital phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Kullorsu: Kullorsuaq Geophysical Observatory (operational by 1991; still active as far as IMAGE/CDAWeb records indicate) is a ground magnetometer station at Kullorsuaq, Greenland, in the high-latitude IMAGE magnetometer network, measuring geomagnetic field variations for ionospheric current, auroral, and magnetospheric studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Tiksi: Tiksi Geophysical Observatory (IAGA TIK), established in 1957 at Tiksi, Sakha Republic, Russia, is a fixed high-latitude Arctic ground observatory, not a spacecraft. It records geomagnetic field variations with fluxgate/absolute magnetometers for ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies; CDAWeb holdings contain available digital magnetometer intervals.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Ranua: Ranua Geophysical Observatory (RAN), operating since at least the early 1980s, is a ground magnetometer station at Ranua, Finland in the IMAGE magnetometer network. It records geomagnetic field variations for studies of ionospheric currents, auroral electrojets, geomagnetic pulsations, and magnetospheric disturbances; it has no orbital phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Carson.C: Carson City Geophysical Observatory was a fixed ground magnetic observatory in Carson City, Nevada, USA; authoritative start/end dates are not clear from the supplied registry. It operated magnetometers measuring local geomagnetic-field variations for geomagnetic, ionospheric, magnetospheric, and space-weather studies, with no orbital or relocation phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/ST5-094: ST5-094 was one of NASA’s three Space Technology 5 microsatellites (launched and operated in 2006) in highly elliptical, near-polar low Earth orbit, about 300–4500 km altitude. It demonstrated miniaturized spacecraft technologies and carried a magnetometer to sample Earth’s magnetosphere/auroral regions; its orbit did not have later mission phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/ISEE2: ISEE 2 was an ESA spacecraft in the NASA/ESA International Sun-Earth Explorer program, launched in 1977 and operated until reentry in 1987. It remained in a highly elliptical geocentric orbit, flying near ISEE 1 with variable separation to study Earth’s magnetosphere, bow shock, magnetopause, upstream solar wind plasma, magnetic fields, waves, and energetic particles.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Qaanaaq: Qaanaaq Geophysical Observatory is a fixed high-latitude ground station at Qaanaaq, northwest Greenland, operating since at least the CDAWeb data era to record geomagnetic field variations with a fluxgate magnetometer for polar ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies; it has no orbital or relocation phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Uummanna: Uummannaq Geophysical Observatory (UMQ) is a ground geomagnetic station at Uummannaq, Greenland, operating since at least the 1970s as part of Greenland high-latitude magnetometer monitoring. It measures local geomagnetic field variations for auroral-zone ionospheric current, substorm, and magnetosphere studies; CDAWeb holdings may cover only selected years.
Repulse Bay Geophysical Observatory is a ground magnetic station at Repulse Bay/Naujaat, Nunavut, Canada, operating in CDAWeb-era records since at least the late 1980s. It has no orbit; it makes fixed-site high-latitude magnetometer measurements of geomagnetic-field variations used for auroral-zone, ionospheric current, substorm, and space-weather studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/3A: BARREL-3A was a NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for RBSP Relativistic Electron Losses payload, launched in Antarctica during the 2015-2016 campaign and ended in 2016. It was a long-duration stratospheric balloon, not an orbiting spacecraft, drifting circumpolarly at ~30-40 km altitude while measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, with magnetometer and GPS/ephemeris support.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Muono: Muono Geophysical Observatory (MUO) is a ground magnetometer station at Muonio, Finnish Lapland, operating in the IMAGE magnetometer network since at least the 1980s. It records local geomagnetic field variations used to study high-latitude ionospheric currents, auroral activity, geomagnetic storms, and substorms; it has no orbital phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/IAGA/Leirvogur: Leirvogur (LRV) is an IAGA ground magnetic observatory in southwest Iceland near Reykjavík, in continuous operation since 1957. It measures local vector geomagnetic field variations and high-latitude magnetic disturbances for ionospheric, magnetospheric, auroral electrojet, and global geomagnetic monitoring studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Derby: Derby Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground geomagnetic station at Derby, Western Australia, operational by the late 20th century in CDAWeb/space-physics archives; no orbit or relocation applies. Its magnetometers measure local geomagnetic field components and variations for ionospheric, magnetospheric, geomagnetic-storm, and space-weather studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Kodiak: Kodiak Geophysical Observatory is a ground magnetometer station on Kodiak Island, Alaska, active in heliophysics data archives at least from the late 20th century, measuring local geomagnetic-field variations for ionospheric, magnetospheric, auroral, and space-weather studies; it has a fixed ground location and no orbital phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Summit: Summit Geophysical Observatory is a ground station at Summit Station on the Greenland ice sheet, operating since at least 1997 in CDAWeb records. It provides fixed high-latitude geomagnetic measurements, chiefly fluxgate magnetometer observations of field variations, for studies of auroral electrodynamics, ionospheric currents, and magnetospheric disturbances; its location has not changed.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Pangnirt: Pangnirtung Geophysical Observatory, operational since about 1993, is a ground geomagnetic station at Pangnirtung, Nunavut, Canada, not a spacecraft. It records geomagnetic field variations with magnetometers for auroral-zone ionospheric and magnetospheric current studies and high-latitude space-weather research, contributing to Canadian geomagnetic data networks.
PENGUIn-5 is a ground-based Antarctic magnetometer station of the PENGUIn polar geospace network, operational during the CDAWeb data era from at least the late 2000s, measuring geomagnetic field variations at the Earth’s surface for studies of auroral-zone ionospheric currents, ULF waves, and magnetospheric dynamics; it has no orbital or relocation phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Dawn: NASA’s Dawn spacecraft (2007-2018) was an ion-propelled planetary mission to the asteroid belt. After heliocentric cruise and a February 2009 Mars gravity-assist flyby, it orbited Vesta from July 2011 to September 2012, then transferred to Ceres, entering orbit in March 2015 and remaining in successive Ceres mapping orbits until mission end in 2018. It measured geology, topography, mineralogy, elemental composition, and ephemeris/trajectory.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Gjoa.Hav: Gjoa Haven Geophysical Observatory (GDH), operating since about 1968 at Gjoa Haven, Nunavut, Canada, is a fixed ground geomagnetic station. It measures vector magnetic-field variations for high-latitude ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies, as part of Canada’s geomagnetic observatory network and contributing INTERMAGNET/CDAWeb data.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/CubeSat/CSSWE: CSSWE (Colorado Student Space Weather Experiment) was a 3U CubeSat launched in 2012 and operated until 2014 in a single low-Earth orbit, about 480 x 780 km at 65° inclination, with gradual orbital decay rather than planned relocations. Its REPTile telescope measured energetic radiation-belt electrons and protons to study space-weather-driven particle dynamics.
Wallops Island Geophysical Observatory is a ground geomagnetic observatory at Wallops Island, Virginia, USA, using magnetometers to measure local magnetic-field variations for ionospheric, magnetospheric, and space-weather studies. It has no orbit; operational start/end dates are not specified in the provided CDAWeb/SPASE context.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Harris: Harris Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground geomagnetic station near Harris, Minnesota, USA (operational start/end not clearly documented in SPASE/CDAWeb). It measures local variations in Earth’s magnetic field with a magnetometer for ionospheric, magnetospheric, and geomagnetic-pulsation studies; its observing vantage point does not change.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/THEMIS/Ground/U: THEMIS-Ground CHBG is the Chibougamau, Quebec, Canada station in the THEMIS/UCLA ground-based observatory network, operating from the 2006-2007 auroral season. It hosts a white-light all-sky imager recording wide-field auroral emissions to study substorm onset and auroral dynamics, coordinated with THEMIS spacecraft observations.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/IAGA/Lucky.Lake: Lucky Lake Magnetometer (IAGA LUC) is a ground-based geomagnetic observatory at Lucky Lake, Saskatchewan, Canada, operational by at least 2008 and apparently active in the INTERMAGNET/CANMOS era. It measures local vector geomagnetic field variations for magnetospheric, ionospheric, and space-weather studies; it has no orbital phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/GOES/9: NOAA GOES-9 was launched in 1995 and supplied CDAWeb space-environment data during 1995-1998. It remained in geostationary Earth orbit, serving as GOES-West near 135°W after checkout, with longitude stationkeeping rather than a new orbital regime. It measured geomagnetic field variations and near-Earth energetic particles using its magnetometer and space environment monitors.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/MetOp/B: MetOp-B (launched 2012, operational 2013-present) is a EUMETSAT polar-orbiting meteorological satellite in a near-circular Sun-synchronous low Earth orbit at about 817 km altitude and 98.7° inclination; its orbit has not substantially changed. For heliophysics it carries NOAA SEM-2 sensors measuring energetic protons and electrons at satellite altitude for radiation belt and space-weather studies.
CLASP2: CLASP2 (Chromospheric LAyer SpectroPolarimeter 2) was a NASA/JAXA/NAOJ/European suborbital solar sounding-rocket experiment launched from White Sands in 2019 and ended after its brief flight. It did not enter orbit; it made minutes of above-atmosphere UV spectropolarimetric observations of the Sun’s lower atmosphere, measuring Mg II h/k and nearby lines plus slit-jaw context to infer chromospheric/photospheric magnetic fields.
FOXSI3: FOXSI-3, the third Focusing Optics X-ray Solar Imager sounding-rocket flight, operated only during a suborbital solar observing flight from White Sands Missile Range on 2018-09-07. It flew above the atmosphere for minutes, not into orbit, using grazing-incidence focusing optics and X-ray detectors to image solar hard X-ray emission from active regions, microflares, and flares.
KSO: Kanzelhöhe Solar Observatory (KSO), University of Graz, began regular solar patrol observations in 1944 from Kanzelhöhe near Villach, Austria (ground based, no orbit). It monitors solar activity with full-disk optical imaging of the photosphere and chromosphere, including white-light sunspots, H-alpha flares/filaments/prominences, and Ca II K plage/network; data are served through VSO.
SOHO: ESA/NASA’s SOHO (launched 1995) is a solar and heliospheric observatory. After launch it transferred to a halo orbit around the Sun–Earth L1 point in early 1996 and has remained an L1 observatory, continuously observing the Sun, corona, CMEs, solar wind, irradiance, helioseismology, energetic particles, and UV/EUV/X-ray emission with instruments including LASCO, EIT, MDI, VIRGO, and CELIAS.
SUNRISE2: SUNRISE2 was the second flight of the SUNRISE balloon-borne solar observatory, operating June 12-17, 2013. Launched from Esrange near Kiruna, Sweden, it flew at stratospheric altitude across the Arctic/Atlantic to northern Canada, observing the solar photosphere and chromosphere with high-resolution UV/visible imaging and magnetography, notably SuFI and IMaX.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Hov.Faro: Hov Faroe Islands Geophysical Observatory (IAGA HOV; operating since 1983, ongoing) is a fixed ground geomagnetic observatory near Hov on Suðuroy, Faroe Islands. It measures Earth’s local magnetic field and variations with magnetometers for ionospheric current, auroral/electrojet, geomagnetic storm, and space-weather studies; no orbital phases apply.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Honolulu: Honolulu Geophysical Observatory (HON), operating since 1902, is a fixed ground geomagnetic observatory on Oahu near Honolulu, Hawaii. It has no orbital phases; magnetometers record local vector/scalar geomagnetic field variations and disturbances for ionospheric, magnetospheric, space-weather, and secular-variation studies, with data distributed via systems such as CDAWeb.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/DynamicsExplore: Dynamics Explorer 2 (DE 2) was a NASA spacecraft launched in 1981 and operated until atmospheric reentry in 1983. It remained in a low-altitude, near-polar, elliptical Earth orbit (initially about 300–1000 km, decaying with time) to study ionosphere-thermosphere electrodynamics, measuring plasma, neutral winds/composition, electric and magnetic fields, and auroral current systems.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Sept.Ile: Sept Iles Geophysical Observatory is a ground geomagnetic station at Sept-Îles, Quebec, Canada, operating since at least 1977, measuring local geomagnetic field variations with magnetometers for ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies. It is fixed on Earth; no orbital or vantage-point phases apply.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Ittoqqor: Ittoqqortoormiit (Scoresbysund) Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground station in East Greenland, operating since at least the early 1980s, with magnetometers measuring local geomagnetic field variations for high-latitude ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies; as a ground observatory it has no orbital phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Priddis: Priddis Geophysical Observatory, operating since 1981 near Priddis, Alberta, Canada, is a ground geophysical site for heliophysics and space-weather studies. It measures local geomagnetic field variations with ground magnetometers, supporting ionospheric current, auroral, and magnetospheric disturbance studies; as a fixed ground observatory it has no orbital phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Pevek: Pevek Geophysical Observatory (opened circa 1957) is a ground-based geomagnetic station at Pevek, Chukotka, Russia, operating high-latitude magnetometers to record geomagnetic field variations, auroral-zone disturbances, magnetic storms, and ionospheric/geospace current systems; it has no orbital phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Puvirnit: Puvirnituq Geophysical Observatory (PBQ), operational since at least 1991 and still active, is a fixed ground magnetometer observatory at Puvirnituq, Nunavik, Quebec, Canada. It records geomagnetic field variations for auroral ionosphere and magnetospheric studies, with data distributed through INTERMAGNET/CDAWeb.
Fort St. John Geophysical Observatory is a ground magnetic observatory at Fort St. John, British Columbia, Canada, operated by Natural Resources Canada for heliophysics and space-weather studies. Since at least the late 20th century it has recorded local geomagnetic field variations with ground magnetometers; as a fixed ground site, it has no orbital phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Giotto: ESA’s Giotto spacecraft (1985-1992) was a heliophysics/comet mission measuring cometary gas, dust, plasma, magnetic fields, and solar-wind interaction. Launched in 1985 into heliocentric cruise, it flew through Comet Halley’s coma in March 1986, hibernated in solar orbit, used an Earth gravity assist in July 1990, then encountered Comet Grigg-Skjellerup in July 1992 before operations ended.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/MAVEN: NASA's MAVEN (Mars Atmosphere and Volatile Evolution; launched 2013, at Mars since 2014) studies Mars' upper atmosphere, ionosphere, solar-wind interaction, escape, plasma and magnetic fields. From 2014-2019 it flew a 4.5-hr highly elliptical Mars orbit (~150 x 6200 km, with periodic deep-dip campaigns to ~125 km); after 2019 aerobraking it has operated in a lower-apoapsis ~3.5-hr elliptical Mars orbit (~150 x 4500 km) while continuing science and relay support.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Loysburg: Loysburg Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground-based magnetometer station at Loysburg, Pennsylvania, USA, operational at least from 2000 in CDAWeb/MEASURE-era holdings; its end date is not confidently documented. It records local geomagnetic field variations for studies of magnetospheric currents, geomagnetic storms/substorms, and space weather, with no orbital or relocation phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Baranov: Baranov Geophysical Observatory is a ground-based high-Arctic geomagnetic station at or near Cape Baranova, Bolshevik Island, Severnaya Zemlya, Russia. It operated at least during the 1980s-1990s, using magnetometers to record local geomagnetic field variations for ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Pine.Rid: Pine Ridge Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground magnetic observatory at Pine Ridge, South Dakota, USA; its operational start and end years are not reliably specified in the SPASE/CDAWeb metadata I can confirm. It measures local geomagnetic-field variations with magnetometers for geospace, ionospheric-current, and space-weather studies; no orbit or relocation applies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Hopen: Hopen Geophysical Observatory (IAGA HOP) is a fixed ground geomagnetic station on Hopen Island, Svalbard, operational by the late 20th century and used in CDAWeb data sets for high-latitude geomagnetic and ionospheric studies. It measures local geomagnetic field variations with magnetometers; there is no orbital or relocation history.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Clyde.Ri: Clyde River Geophysical Observatory (operational by 1992; end not clearly specified in SPASE/CDAWeb records) is a fixed ground magnetometer site at Clyde River, Nunavut, Canada. It records geomagnetic field variations for high-latitude ionospheric, auroral, cusp, and magnetospheric studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Shawano: Shawano Geophysical Observatory is a ground-based fluxgate magnetometer station at Shawano, Wisconsin, USA, with CDAWeb data beginning in 2006 and no confirmed end year. It measures local three-component geomagnetic field variations and ULF perturbations for studies of ionospheric currents, substorms, and magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling; its observing location is fixed on the ground.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Cluster: ESA’s Cluster mission (launched 2000; science operations 2001-2024) was four spacecraft in coordinated highly elliptical polar Earth orbits, with varying spacecraft separations and evolving local-time coverage. It measured magnetospheric plasma, magnetic/electric fields, waves, and energetic particles in the magnetosphere, magnetosheath, bow shock, and sometimes upstream solar wind.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Phobos2: Phobos 2 (USSR, launched 1988; contact lost March 1989) studied Mars, Phobos, and the solar-wind interaction with Mars with imaging, plasma/ion, magnetic-field, energetic-particle, and wave instruments. It cruised heliocentrically from Earth to Mars in 1988-Jan 1989, entered a highly elliptical Mars orbit in Jan-Feb 1989, then maneuvered in Feb-Mar 1989 into a near-equatorial, near-Phobos-synchronous Mars orbit for Phobos approach operations.
Trapper Creek Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground magnetic station at Trapper Creek, Alaska, in operation in the THEMIS/CDAWeb era from at least the late 2000s. It measures local geomagnetic field variations with a ground magnetometer for studies of auroral-zone ionospheric currents and magnetospheric activity; it has no orbital or relocation phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Kangerlu: Kangerlussuaq Geophysical Observatory, at Kangerlussuaq/Søndre Strømfjord in western Greenland (about 67°N, 51°W), is a ground high-latitude observatory operational since at least 1977. Its magnetometers measure local geomagnetic-field variations for studies of auroral ionospheric currents, substorms, and magnetospheric dynamics; it has no orbit.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Rorvik: Rørvik Geophysical Observatory (IAGA RVK, operating since about 1985) is a fixed ground-based geomagnetic observatory at Rørvik, Norway, not a spacecraft. It records local vector geomagnetic field variations for studies of ionospheric currents, auroral electrojets, magnetic storms, substorms, and magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling; its observing location has not changed.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/CRRES: CRRES (Combined Release and Radiation Effects Satellite) was a U.S. Air Force/NASA mission launched in 1990 and operated until failure in 1991. It remained in a highly elliptical geocentric transfer orbit, about 350 x 33,500 km at ~18° inclination, sampling the inner magnetosphere and radiation belts with particle, field, wave, and radiation-effects instruments, and conducting active chemical-release experiments.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Sanikilu: Sanikiluaq Geophysical Observatory (Sanikiluaq, Nunavut, Canada; operational in CDAWeb at least from 2006) is a fixed ground-based high-latitude station in the Canadian/THEMIS-CARISMA geomagnetic network, measuring local magnetic-field variations for auroral ionosphere and magnetosphere studies; it has no orbital phases.
PENGUIn-4 is a ground geophysical observatory in Antarctica in the PENGUIn network, operating from at least the 2000s, using a magnetometer to record geomagnetic field variations for studies of polar ionospheric currents, substorms, ULF waves, and magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling; it has no orbital phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Bettles: Bettles Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground station at Bettles, Alaska, USA (no orbit; operational start and end are not reliably documented in this summary, but it appears in historical CDAWeb/SPASE high-latitude records). It measures local geomagnetic-field variations with ground magnetometers for auroral, ionospheric-current, and magnetospheric studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Stanford: Stanford Geophysical Observatory is a ground geomagnetic station at Stanford University, California; its exact operational start/end year is not confirmed in the registry, but it is a fixed ground site with no orbital or vantage-point changes. It operates a fluxgate magnetometer measuring local geomagnetic-field variations for ionospheric, magnetospheric, ULF-wave, and space-weather studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Hornepay: Hornepayne Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground magnetometer site at Hornepayne, Ontario, Canada, operational at least during CDAWeb holdings in the 2010s, measuring local geomagnetic-field variations for ionospheric current, substorm, and magnetospheric studies; it has no orbital or relocation phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Gakona: The Gakona Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground site near Gakona, Alaska, USA, operational since the late 1990s and represented in CDAWeb for ground magnetometer data. It measures local geomagnetic field variations from auroral electrojets, ionospheric currents, and magnetospheric disturbances; as a ground station it has no orbital phases or changing vantage point.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Igloolik: Igloolik Geophysical Observatory is a ground-based geomagnetic station at Igloolik, Nunavut, Canada, operational from at least the early 1990s, with no well-documented end year in the registry. It has no orbit; it records local magnetic-field variations for high-latitude ionospheric, auroral, cusp, and magnetospheric studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Petersbu: Petersburg Geophysical Observatory is a ground-based geomagnetic station in St. Petersburg, Russia, operating at least during the CDAWeb digital data era (1990s–present; exact start not verified here). It measures local geomagnetic field variations with magnetometers for ionospheric, magnetospheric, and space-weather studies; it has no orbital phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Whitehor: Whitehorse Geophysical Observatory (WHI), operating since 1957 in Whitehorse, Yukon, Canada, is a fixed ground magnetic observatory with no orbital phases. It measures geomagnetic field variations with magnetometers for ionospheric, auroral, magnetospheric, and space-weather studies and contributes data to networks such as INTERMAGNET.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Munin: Munin was a Swedish microsatellite (launched 2000; science operations ended in 2001) in a low-Earth near-polar orbit throughout its mission, with no known major orbital relocation. It studied auroral and magnetospheric plasma processes, wave–particle interactions, and space weather; MEDUSA measured energetic neutral atoms and charged particles in near-Earth geospace.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Alouette2: Alouette 2 was a Canadian topside-sounder satellite launched in 1965 and operated until 1975. It remained in a near-polar, highly elliptical Earth orbit, about 500 km perigee, 3,000 km apogee, and 80° inclination, sounding the topside ionosphere and lower plasmasphere with radio instruments and in situ plasma measurements of electron density and ionospheric structure.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/GOLD: NASA’s GOLD (Global-scale Observations of the Limb and Disk), launched in 2018 and in science operations since 2018, is a far-ultraviolet imaging spectrograph hosted on the SES-14 communications satellite in geostationary orbit near 47.5°W over the Americas. Its vantage has not changed; it images Earth’s thermosphere and ionosphere via disk and limb airglow.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Pello: Pello Geophysical Observatory (PEL; operating since 1973) is a fixed ground-based magnetometer station at Pello, northern Finland, now part of the IMAGE magnetometer network. It records geomagnetic field variations used to study ionospheric currents, auroral electrojets, geomagnetic pulsations, and magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling; its observing location has not changed.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/ISEE3: ISEE-3/ICE (International Sun-Earth Explorer 3, launched 1978; operations ended 1997) measured solar wind plasma, interplanetary magnetic fields, energetic particles, cosmic rays, and waves. It occupied a Sun-Earth L1 halo orbit in 1978-1982; after lunar flyby maneuvers in 1982-1983 it made distant geomagnetic-tail observations, then a Dec 1983 lunar swingby put it in heliocentric orbit for comet Giacobini-Zinner (1985), Halley-era, and heliospheric studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Worthing: Worthington Geophysical Observatory was a ground magnetic observatory in Worthington, Minnesota, USA, operating at least in the late 20th-century CDAWeb/SPASE archive era; its exact start and end years are not confirmed here. It was not a spacecraft and had no orbital phases, measuring local geomagnetic field variations with magnetometers for geomagnetic, ionospheric, and space-weather studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Snap.Lak: Snap Lake Geophysical Observatory (operational by 2006; end date not identified) is a ground geomagnetic station near Snap Lake, Northwest Territories, Canada, represented in CDAWeb/THEMIS-GMAG holdings as SNKQ. It measures local magnetic-field variations for auroral, ionospheric, and magnetospheric studies; it has no orbital phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Attu: Attu Geophysical Observatory (ATU) was a USGS ground magnetic observatory on Attu Island in the Aleutian Islands, Alaska, operated in the mid-20th century and represented in CDAWeb for geomagnetic field time series. It measured high-latitude magnetic variations for ionospheric, magnetospheric, auroral, and geomagnetic storm studies; it had no orbital motion.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Pueblo: Pueblo Geophysical Observatory is a ground magnetic observatory in Pueblo, Colorado, USA; its exact operational start/end dates are not confidently identified here. It provides fixed-site magnetometer measurements of local geomagnetic field variations for heliophysics, geomagnetic-storm, and ionospheric-current studies, with no orbital or relocation phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Coral.Ha: Coral Harbour Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground magnetometer station at Coral Harbour (Salliq), Southampton Island, Nunavut, Canada, operational in the space-physics data record from at least 1992. It measures local geomagnetic field variations for high-latitude auroral, ionospheric-current, and magnetospheric studies; there is no spacecraft orbit.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/ISIS1: ISIS 1 (International Satellites for Ionospheric Studies; launched 1969, operated until 1984) was a Canadian/NASA ionospheric satellite in a highly inclined eccentric low-Earth orbit (~578 x 3526 km, ~88°). Its orbit had no planned relocation; it sampled the topside ionosphere and inner plasmasphere with a swept-frequency topside sounder, VLF/ELF receivers, and plasma/particle instruments.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/1N: BARREL-1N was a NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for RBSP Relativistic Electron Losses stratospheric balloon payload flown in the 2012-2013 Antarctic BARREL campaign. Drifting at roughly 30-40 km over Antarctica, it measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation and local magnetic/ULF wave signatures in conjunction with the Van Allen Probes.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/4B: BARREL-4B was a NASA/Dartmouth BARREL high-altitude balloon payload, launched and ended in 2016 during an Arctic stratospheric campaign from Esrange near Kiruna, Sweden, not an orbital spacecraft. It studied geospace radiation-belt electron precipitation by measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays with scintillator detectors, with GPS and ancillary field/housekeeping data for Van Allen Probes conjunctions.
spase://NASA/Observatory/AeroCube-6/B: AeroCube-6B (AC6-B) was one of two Aerospace Corp./NSF CubeSats launched in 2014 into near-circular polar low Earth orbit, operating through 2017. It carried dosimeters to measure energetic electron/proton radiation in the inner magnetosphere and radiation belts, especially relativistic electron microbursts; its observing vantage remained LEO, with changing separation from AC6-A enabling two-point studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Kuujjuaq: Kuujjuaq Geophysical Observatory, operated by NRCan/CANMOS in Kuujjuaq, Quebec, Canada, is a fixed ground geomagnetic observatory, operational since about 1981 and ongoing, measuring vector geomagnetic field variations with magnetometers for auroral-zone, ionospheric current, magnetic storm, and magnetospheric studies; it has no orbital phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Radisson: Radisson Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground magnetometer station at Radisson, Quebec, Canada, used in Canadian geospace monitoring and archived in CDAWeb. It measures geomagnetic field variations for ionospheric current and magnetospheric disturbance studies; there is no spacecraft orbit or changing vantage point. Operational start/end are not confidently verified here.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Americus: Americus Geophysical Observatory (operational in CDAWeb ground-magnetometer records from about 2005/2006 onward; end date not confirmed) is a fixed station in Americus, Georgia, USA. It measures local geomagnetic field variations for heliophysics studies of ionospheric and magnetospheric currents, geomagnetic storms, substorms, and ULF waves; its location has not changed.
PENGUIn-2 (operational start uncertain; active in CDAWeb-era Antarctic campaigns) is a ground-based magnetometer station in Antarctica within the Polar Earth Observing Network for Geospace Upper-atmosphere Investigations. It has no orbit; it records local geomagnetic field variations used to study polar ionospheric currents, substorms, and magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Savissiv: Savissivik Geophysical Observatory is a ground magnetometer station at Savissivik, northwest Greenland, operational since at least the 1990s in CDAWeb records. It measures local geomagnetic field variations for high-latitude ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies; as a fixed ground site, it has no orbital phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Val.d.Or: Val-d'Or Geophysical Observatory is a ground magnetic station at Val-d'Or, Quebec, Canada; its exact operational start/end are not confidently established here. It records local geomagnetic field variations with ground magnetometers for ionospheric, magnetospheric, and geomagnetic disturbance studies, with no orbital or vantage-point changes.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Thule.Ai: Thule Air Base Geophysical Observatory at Pituffik/Thule, northwest Greenland, is a fixed high-Arctic ground observatory operating since at least the 1980s CDAWeb era. It measures local geomagnetic-field variations with a ground magnetometer to study polar-cap ionospheric currents, geomagnetic disturbances, and magnetosphere–ionosphere coupling; its observing location has not changed.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Bjorn: Bjorn is a ground geomagnetic observatory on Bjørnøya/Bear Island, Norway, in the high-latitude Arctic, hosting a magnetometer that records local geomagnetic field variations for ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies; its precise operational start/end dates and network affiliation are not confirmed in the supplied metadata.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Solund: Solund Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground geomagnetic station at Solund on Norway’s west coast, operating since about 1996 with no orbital motion or relocation. It records local magnetic-field variations using a ground magnetometer for ionospheric, auroral-current, and magnetospheric studies, with data distributed through networks archived in CDAWeb.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Kapuskas: Kapuskasing Geophysical Observatory (IAGA KAP), established in the late 1960s and still active, is a fixed ground magnetic observatory near Kapuskasing, Ontario, Canada. It has no orbital phases; it records geomagnetic field components and variations with magnetometers for ionospheric, magnetospheric, and space-weather studies, as part of Canada’s observatory network and INTERMAGNET.
PENGUIn-0 (PG0) is a ground geophysical observatory at/near Amundsen–Scott South Pole Station, Antarctica, operational by the 2010s, measuring geomagnetic field variations with a magnetometer for polar ionospheric, magnetospheric, and space-weather studies; it is a fixed ground site, not an orbital mission.

PENGUIn-3 is a ground geophysical observatory in Antarctica, part of the PENGUIn high-latitude geospace network, operational by the 2007–2008 IPY era. It uses ground magnetometers to record geomagnetic field variations for studies of polar ionospheric currents, auroral electrodynamics, and magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling; it has no orbit or moving vantage point.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Dededo: Dededo Geophysical Observatory (Guam; operational since about 1957 and active in modern CDAWeb/INTERMAGNET-era holdings) is a fixed ground magnetic observatory, not a spacecraft. It measures local geomagnetic field vector/intensity variations with magnetometers for ionospheric, magnetospheric, geomagnetic storm, and space-weather studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Red.Deer: Red Deer Geophysical Observatory is a ground magnetometer site at Red Deer, Alberta, Canada, used for ionospheric, magnetospheric, and space-weather studies by measuring local geomagnetic field variations. It is associated with Canadian ground magnetic networks and CDAWeb holdings; its observing site/vantage is fixed, not orbital.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Kevo: Kevo Geophysical Observatory (KEV), in Kevo/Utsjoki, northern Finland, is a fixed ground station, not a spacecraft. Operating since the IGY-era and in the IMAGE magnetometer network from the early 1980s, it records geomagnetic field variations for auroral-zone ionospheric and magnetospheric studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Narsarsu: Narsarsuaq Geophysical Observatory (NAQ), operating since the IGY era (about 1957), is a ground station in southern Greenland near 61.2°N, 45.4°W. It has no orbit; it records local geomagnetic-field variations with magnetometers for ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies and contributes to Greenland/high-latitude monitoring networks.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Salluit: Salluit Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground magnetic station at Salluit, Nunavik, Quebec, Canada; the registry/data-system records do not give a confidently verified operational start or end year. It uses a fluxgate magnetometer to record geomagnetic field variations for high-latitude ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies, and has no orbital phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Laurel: Laurel Geophysical Observatory (operational start not confirmed; CDAWeb holdings document 20th-century use) is a ground-based geomagnetic station in Laurel, Maryland, USA. It operates magnetometers measuring local Earth magnetic-field variations for ionospheric, magnetospheric, geomagnetic-storm, and pulsation studies; it has no orbital phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Karmoy: Karmøy Geophysical Observatory (Karmøy, Norway; magnetometer operations began in 1983 and continue in the CDAWeb/SMWG record, with exact end/status not independently confirmed) is a fixed ground station measuring local geomagnetic field variations for ionospheric current, substorm, geomagnetic-storm, and magnetospheric studies; it has no orbital phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Colville: The Colville National Forest/Newport geomagnetic observatory in northeastern Washington, USA, is a fixed ground station operating since about 1966. It measures vector geomagnetic field variations for studies of ionospheric and magnetospheric current systems, geomagnetic storms, and space-weather disturbances; there are no orbital or vantage-point changes.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/La.Ronge: La Ronge Geophysical Observatory is a ground magnetometer site at La Ronge, Saskatchewan, Canada; it has no orbit. Operational dates are not fully verified, but CDAWeb holdings include THEMIS-era data from about 2006 onward. It records geomagnetic field variations for auroral currents, substorms, ULF waves, and magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling studies.
STEREO_B: NASA’s STEREO-B (Behind) spacecraft, launched in 2006, studied CMEs, solar wind, heliospheric structure, particles/fields, radio bursts, and solar/heliospheric imaging (SECCHI, IMPACT, PLASTIC, S/WAVES). In 2006-early 2007 it flew highly elliptical Earth phasing orbits with lunar flybys; from 2007 until loss of routine science contact in 2014 it was in a heliocentric orbit just outside Earth’s, progressively trailing Earth.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/THEMIS/C: THEMIS-C (launched 2007), later ARTEMIS-P2, carries plasma, energetic-particle, field and wave instruments for magnetospheric and lunar/heliospheric science. From 2007-2010 it flew a highly elliptical Earth orbit as an outer THEMIS probe sampling the magnetotail and inner magnetosphere; in 2010-2011 it used lunar flybys and Earth-Moon Lagrange transfer orbits, then from 2011 onward has orbited the Moon.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Cluster-Rumba: Cluster-Rumba (Cluster 1/FM5) is one of ESA’s four Cluster II spacecraft, launched in 2000 and operated for science until 2024. It remained in a highly elliptical, near-polar Earth orbit throughout the mission, with evolving apogee/perigee geometry and variable formation separations, measuring fields, waves, plasma, and energetic particles in the magnetosphere, bow shock, magnetosheath, and solar wind.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/MMS/1: MMS-1, one of NASA’s four Magnetospheric Multiscale spacecraft (launched 2015, operating), studies magnetic reconnection, turbulence, and particle acceleration with high-rate fields and plasma instruments. It flew a highly elliptical Earth orbit with apogee near 12 RE in 2015-early 2017 for dayside magnetopause/near-tail campaigns; from 2017 its apogee was raised to about 25 RE for deeper magnetotail seasons while continuing magnetopause crossings.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Cluster-Salsa: Cluster-Salsa (C2/FM6) was one of ESA’s four Cluster II spacecraft, launched in 2000 and operated until its controlled reentry in 2024. Throughout the mission it flew a highly elliptical polar Earth orbit in formation with the other Cluster spacecraft, with separations adjusted for multi-point sampling, to study the magnetosphere, bow shock, magnetopause, aurora, plasma particles, fields, and waves.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Cluster-Tango: ESA’s Cluster-Tango (C4, launched 2000; science operations 2001-2024) was one of four Cluster spacecraft in evolving, highly elliptical near-polar Earth orbit throughout the mission, with controlled inter-spacecraft separations. It measured magnetic/electric fields, waves, plasma, and energetic particles in the magnetosphere, cusps, magnetotail, magnetopause, bow shock, and solar wind.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/MMS/3: MMS-3 (launched 2015) is one of NASA’s four Magnetospheric Multiscale spacecraft, providing high-time-resolution fields, plasma, and energetic-particle data for magnetic reconnection, acceleration, and turbulence. It flew in a close tetrahedral formation in highly elliptical Earth orbit: 2015-early 2017 at about 1.2 x 12 RE for dayside magnetopause studies, then from 2017 onward after apogee raising to about 25 RE for magnetotail and broader magnetospheric campaigns.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Cluster-Samba: Cluster-Samba (ESA Cluster II spacecraft 3, launched 2000; science operations ended 2024) flew with the four-spacecraft Cluster constellation in highly elliptical, near-polar Earth orbits throughout the mission, with inter-spacecraft separations varied for campaigns. It measured Earth’s magnetosphere, bow shock, magnetopause, aurora, plasma, fields, waves, and energetic particles using instruments such as FGM, CIS, PEACE, EFW, STAFF, WHISPER, and RAPID.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/THEMIS/A: THEMIS-A (THA), launched in 2007, is a NASA THEMIS spacecraft for magnetospheric substorm studies. After launch and 2007 orbit phasing, it has remained in a highly elliptical, near-equatorial geocentric orbit sampling the inner/near-Earth magnetosphere and magnetotail, measuring electric and magnetic fields, plasma, and energetic particles with EFI, FGM/SCM, ESA, and SST; it was not transferred to lunar ARTEMIS.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/MMS/4: MMS-4 is one of NASA’s four Magnetospheric Multiscale spacecraft (launched 2015, operating), measuring 3-D plasma distributions, energetic particles, and electric/magnetic fields. It began in a near-equatorial highly elliptical Earth orbit with apogee near 12 Re for dayside magnetopause encounters in 2015-2016; in 2017 apogee was raised to about 25 Re for magnetotail science, with later extended phases sampling the magnetopause, bow shock, magnetosheath, and tail.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/RBSP/A: RBSP-A (Van Allen Probe A; launched 2012, science operations ended 2019) studied Earth’s Van Allen radiation belts and inner magnetosphere. Throughout the mission it flew a highly elliptical, low-inclination near-equatorial Earth orbit repeatedly sampling perigee-to-apogee regions through the belts; only end-of-mission perigee-lowering maneuvers occurred in 2019. Instruments measured fields, waves, energetic particles, and radiation.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/THEMIS/B: THEMIS-B, renamed ARTEMIS P1, is a NASA probe launched in 2007 to measure magnetospheric/substorm plasma, fields, waves, and particles. It flew highly elliptical Earth orbits for THEMIS magnetotail science from 2007-2009, then used lunar-transfer trajectories in 2009-2010, operated near the Earth-Moon L2/L1 regions in 2010-2011, and entered lunar orbit in 2011, where it continues lunar/solar-wind plasma and fields observations.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/STEREO-A: STEREO-A (launched 2006) studies CMEs, solar wind, magnetic fields, radio bursts, and energetic particles with SECCHI, IMPACT, PLASTIC, and S/WAVES. It spent launch–Dec 2006 in highly elliptical Earth phasing orbits with a lunar flyby, then entered a heliocentric orbit slightly inside Earth’s orbit, drifting ahead of Earth; it lapped Earth with a close flyby in 2023 and continues heliocentric observations.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/THEMIS/E: THEMIS-E (Probe E/P4), launched in 2007, is one of NASA’s THEMIS substorm spacecraft. After 2007 commissioning and orbit placement, it has remained in a near-equatorial, highly elliptical geocentric orbit (inner THEMIS probe, about 1-day period with magnetospheric apogee), measuring electric and magnetic fields, plasma, and energetic particles in Earth’s plasma sheet and inner magnetosphere.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/SOHO: ESA/NASA’s SOHO (launched Dec. 1995) is a solar/heliospheric observatory. After launch and transfer to the Sun-Earth L1 region in Dec. 1995-Feb. 1996, it has operated in a halo orbit about L1, observing the solar interior, photosphere, corona, CMEs, solar wind, and energetic particles with instruments such as LASCO, EIT, MDI, CELIAS, COSTEP, and ERNE.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/STEREO-B: STEREO-B (Behind), launched 2006, was NASA’s trailing Solar Terrestrial Relations Observatory spacecraft. In late 2006–early 2007 it used highly elliptical Earth phasing orbits with lunar flybys, then entered a heliocentric orbit drifting behind Earth, observing solar eruptions and the heliosphere with SECCHI, IMPACT, PLASTIC, and S/WAVES until contact was lost in 2014.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/RBSP/B: RBSP-B (Van Allen Probe B), launched in 2012 and operated until July 2019, studied Earth’s radiation belts and inner magnetosphere with energetic-particle, fields, and wave instruments. It flew a near-equatorial, highly elliptical geocentric orbit from 2012 to early 2019; in 2019 disposal maneuvers lowered perigee before shutdown, while observations continued.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Cluster/C1: Cluster-C1 (Rumba), launched in 2000 and operated for science until 2024, was one of ESA’s four Cluster spacecraft in a highly elliptical near-polar Earth orbit throughout the mission. It sampled the magnetosphere, magnetosheath, bow shock, cusp, auroral regions, and solar wind with plasma, magnetic-field, electric-field, energetic-particle, and wave instruments.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Ground/Benningt: Bennington is a ground-based geomagnetic station in Bennington, Vermont, USA, used in the THEMIS/GMAG ground network. Operational in CDAWeb from about 2006 with no orbital phases, it measures local vector geomagnetic-field variations for studies of ionospheric currents, substorms, and magnetosphere–ionosphere coupling.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/SolarOrbiter: ESA/NASA’s Solar Orbiter (launched 2020) studies the Sun and inner heliosphere with remote-sensing imagers/spectrometers and in-situ plasma, fields and particle instruments. It has always been in heliocentric orbit: 2020-2021 was cruise/commissioning with Venus flybys in Dec 2020 and Aug 2021 and an Earth flyby in Nov 2021; since late 2021 it has used repeated Venus assists to lower perihelion toward ~0.28 AU and raise inclination for out-of-ecliptic solar views.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/Cluster/C3: Cluster-C3 (Samba) was one of ESA’s four Cluster II spacecraft, launched in 2000 and operated for magnetospheric science until 2024. It remained in a highly elliptical, near-polar Earth orbit throughout, with evolving apogee/perigee and spacecraft separations, sampling the magnetosphere, magnetotail, cusps, bow shock, and solar wind using plasma, field, wave, and energetic-particle instruments.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/MMS/2: MMS-2 is one of NASA’s four Magnetospheric Multiscale spacecraft, launched in 2015 to study magnetic reconnection, turbulence, and particle acceleration with high-rate plasma, fields, and energetic-particle instruments. In 2015-2016 it flew a highly elliptical Earth orbit of about 1.2 x 12 RE targeting the dayside magnetopause; in 2017 its apogee was raised to about 25 RE for magnetotail campaigns, continuing in this high-apogee geocentric orbit.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/LANL/2002: LANL-2002 was a Los Alamos National Laboratory geosynchronous spacecraft operating from 2002 to 2008 at GEO, with no known major orbit change. It supported magnetospheric and space-weather studies; its Magnetospheric Plasma Analyzer (MPA) measured 3D ion and electron energy-per-charge distributions in the near-Earth plasma environment.
FOXSI2: FOXSI-2, the second Focusing Optics X-ray Solar Imager sounding-rocket flight, operated only on 2014-12-11 during a brief ballistic suborbital launch from White Sands Missile Range. It observed the Sun above the atmosphere with grazing-incidence focusing optics and hard X-ray detectors to image faint coronal X-ray emission related to flares, particle acceleration, and coronal heating.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/GOES/6: NOAA’s GOES-6 satellite (1983-1994) was a geostationary Earth-orbiting observatory, repositioned among operational GOES longitudes but remaining near GEO throughout its mission. It monitored space weather at ~6.6 Earth radii with magnetometer and energetic-particle sensors measuring the geomagnetic field and magnetospheric particle environment.
STEREO_A: STEREO-A, launched in 2006, studies CMEs, solar eruptions, solar wind, energetic particles, and heliospheric structure with SECCHI, IMPACT, PLASTIC, and S/WAVES. After brief geocentric phasing orbits and a lunar gravity assist in Dec 2006, it entered a ~1 AU heliocentric orbit drifting ahead of Earth by about 22°/yr; it remained in this orbit through solar conjunction and returned near Earth in Aug 2023 after one full lap.
SUNRISE1: SUNRISE-1 was a stratospheric balloon solar observatory on a single June 2009 flight, launched from ESRANGE near Kiruna, Sweden, and drifting west across the Arctic at about 35–37 km before recovery in northern Canada. It observed photospheric and chromospheric fine structure and magnetic fields at high spatial resolution, using instruments such as SuFI and IMaX.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/GOES/10: GOES-10 (NOAA; launched 1997, operational 1998-2009) was a geostationary Earth weather and space-environment satellite. It served at about 135°W as GOES-West from 1998 to 2006, then was relocated to about 60°W from 2006 until retirement in 2009. Its SEM package measured magnetic fields, energetic particles, and solar X-rays for magnetospheric and space-weather studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/GOES/11: NOAA GOES-11 (launched 2000; operational GOES service 2006-2011) was a geostationary Earth-orbit weather satellite carrying space-weather sensors for solar X-rays, energetic particles, and the local geomagnetic field. It remained in geostationary orbit as an on-orbit spare before becoming GOES-West near 135°W in 2006; it was retired to graveyard orbit in December 2011.
GOES-12: NOAA’s GOES-12 (GOES-M, launched 2001; operational 2003-2013) was a geostationary environmental satellite for solar and space-weather monitoring. After geostationary checkout/storage in 2001-2003, it served as GOES-East near 75°W from 2003 to May 2010, then relocated near 60°W for South America coverage until 2013. It carried SXI for full-disk soft-X-ray coronal imaging plus XRS/EPS space-environment sensors.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/GOES/13: NOAA’s GOES-13 (launched 2006; NOAA operational 2010-2017) was a geostationary Earth/space-weather satellite. After checkout and on-orbit storage near 105°W in 2006-2010, it served as GOES-East near 75°W from 2010 to Dec 2017, measuring geosynchronous energetic particles, magnetic field, solar X-rays/EUV, and Earth weather imagery.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/GOES/14: NOAA GOES-14 (launched 2009, operated to 2020) was a geostationary Earth-orbit weather and space-environment satellite. It remained in geostationary orbit throughout, with checkout/storage and backup operations at changing longitudes, including around 105°W and temporary GOES-East service near 75°W in 2012–2013. EPS, MAG, and SEM/XRS monitored energetic particles, magnetic fields, and solar X-ray/EUV conditions.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/GOES/15: NOAA’s GOES-15 (launched 2010; operated 2010-2020) was a geostationary environmental satellite. After checkout/storage near 90°W in 2010-2011, it served as GOES-West near 135°W from late 2011 to 2018, then operated in a supplemental/standby role near 128°W until decommissioning in 2020. MAG, EPS/HEPAD, SEM, and XRS measured magnetic fields, energetic particles, and solar X-rays.
GOES16: GOES-16 (GOES-R), launched in 2016 and operational from 2017, is a NOAA geostationary satellite. It completed checkout near 89.5°W in 2016–2017, served as GOES-East near 75.2°W from Dec 2017 to Apr 2025, then moved to on-orbit standby/storage. It carries SUVI for full-disk solar EUV imaging plus EXIS, SEISS, and MAG for solar irradiance, energetic particles, and fields.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/GOES/16: GOES-16 (launched 2016; operational 2017-present) is a NOAA GOES-R geostationary satellite for weather and space-environment monitoring. After checkout near 89.5°W in 2017, it served as GOES-East at about 75.2°W from Dec 2017 to Apr 2025, measuring solar X-ray/EUV irradiance (EXIS), energetic particles (SEISS), and magnetic fields.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/GOES/17: NOAA’s GOES-17 (launched 2018, ended 2023) was a geostationary GOES-R series weather and space-environment satellite. It checked out near 89.5°W in 2018, served as GOES-West at 137.2°W from 2019 to Jan 2023, then drifted to on-orbit storage near 105°W before retirement. Heliophysics sensors included MAG, EXIS, SEISS, and SUVI for fields, particles, solar X-rays/EUV, and solar imaging.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/GOES/7: GOES-7 (launched 1987, operated until 1996) was a NOAA geostationary weather and space-environment satellite. It remained in geostationary Earth orbit but was relocated in longitude: initially serving GOES-West near 135°W, after GOES-6’s 1989 failure moved to a central/East coverage slot near 98°W through 1995, then backup service until decommissioning. Its Space Environment Monitor measured local magnetic field, energetic particles, and solar X-rays.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/GOES/8: GOES-8 (launched 1994; operational 1995-2003) was a NOAA geostationary GOES-East satellite near 75°W longitude. It monitored Earth’s near-geosynchronous magnetospheric environment with magnetometer and energetic-particle sensors, plus space-weather solar X-ray observations; its science vantage remained geostationary until replacement and retirement in 2003.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/LANL/1991: LANL-1991 was a Los Alamos National Laboratory geosynchronous spacecraft launched in 1991 and operated through 2008, monitoring the near-Earth magnetosphere from GEO for its full mission. Its MPA and SOPA particle instruments measured magnetospheric plasma and energetic electron/ion fluxes, widely used for radiation-belt, substorm, and space-weather studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/LANL/2001: LANL-2001 was a Los Alamos geosynchronous Earth-orbit spacecraft, operational in 2001-2008, with no major orbit changes; it sampled the near-equatorial magnetosphere at GEO. Its Magnetospheric Plasma Analyzer (MPA) measured 3D ion and electron energy-per-charge distributions for magnetospheric plasma and space-weather studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/2N: BARREL-2N was a NASA/Dartmouth stratospheric balloon payload launched and operated in the 2015 Northern Hemisphere BARREL campaign from Esrange/Kiruna, Sweden, drifting in the polar stratosphere. It measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, with magnetic-field and GPS/ephemeris data, to study magnetospheric loss processes.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/1G: BARREL-1G was a NASA/Dartmouth BARREL high-altitude balloon payload that flew during the 2013 Antarctic campaign, drifting in the stratospheric circumpolar vortex rather than orbiting Earth. It measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, with magnetometer and GPS/ephemeris data, for conjugate studies with the Van Allen Probes.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/2I: BARREL-2I was one payload in NASA’s BARREL Antarctic balloon array, flown in 2014 during the second BARREL campaign. It was a stratospheric circumpolar balloon over Antarctica/Southern Ocean, not an orbiting spacecraft, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation plus local magnetic fields to study magnetospheric loss processes.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/1M: BARREL-1M was an individual Balloon Array for RBSP Relativistic Electron Losses stratospheric balloon payload flown during the 2013 Antarctic BARREL campaign. Drifting at near-space balloon altitudes over Antarctica, it measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from precipitating radiation-belt electrons and local magnetic fields to study electron loss and magnetospheric wave-particle interactions.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/2L: BARREL-2L was one payload of NASA’s Balloon Array for RBSP Relativistic Electron Losses, operated during the second Antarctic balloon campaign in 2013-2014. It was a stratospheric long-duration balloon launched from Antarctica and drifting in the southern polar vortex, carrying X-ray/gamma-ray and magnetic-field instruments to measure radiation-belt electron precipitation and magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/3D: BARREL-3D was a NASA/Dartmouth BARREL stratospheric balloon payload flown in the 2015-2016 Antarctic campaign, drifting at high altitude over Antarctica rather than orbiting Earth. It measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, with supporting magnetometer and ephemeris data, to study magnetospheric loss processes in conjunction with Van Allen Probes.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/2D: BARREL-2D was a specific Balloon Array for RBSP Relativistic Electron Losses payload flown in the second Antarctic campaign (2013-2014). It was a high-altitude, long-duration stratospheric balloon over Antarctica, not an orbital spacecraft, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays from precipitating radiation-belt electrons, with GPS/ephemeris and magnetic-field context for Van Allen Probes conjunction studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/4F: BARREL-4F (launched and ended in 2016) was a NASA BARREL high-altitude balloon payload from the fourth campaign, flown from the Esrange/Kiruna Arctic balloon base in Sweden rather than orbit. It drifted in the stratosphere measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, supporting studies of electron loss and magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/2T: BARREL-2T was a NASA Balloon Array for RBSP Relativistic Electron Losses stratospheric balloon payload from the second Antarctic BARREL campaign, operating during its 2014 flight over Antarctica/Southern Ocean at roughly 30–40 km altitude. It measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, with magnetometer and GPS/ephemeris data supporting Van Allen Probes studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/2K: BARREL-2K was a NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses long-duration stratospheric balloon payload, launched and ended in 2014 during the Antarctic campaign. It drifted at balloon altitude over Antarctica rather than orbiting, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays from precipitating radiation-belt electrons, with magnetometer and GPS context.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/5A: BARREL-5A was a NASA/Dartmouth BARREL stratospheric balloon payload operated during a single Antarctic long-duration balloon flight in the Van Allen Probes era (2013–2014 campaign period; exact flight dates should be verified). Flying at roughly 30–40 km over Antarctica, it measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation for magnetospheric loss studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/2Q: BARREL-2Q was a NASA/Dartmouth BARREL high-altitude balloon payload in the Antarctic stratosphere during the 2014 BARREL campaign, drifting with circumpolar winds rather than orbiting. It measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, with magnetometer and GPS/ephemeris data, for magnetospheric and space-weather studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/4D: BARREL-4D was a NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses stratospheric balloon payload, launched and operated in 2016 during BARREL's fourth campaign from Esrange near Kiruna, Sweden. Floating at ~30-40 km over the Arctic/subauroral region, it measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from precipitating radiation-belt electrons for radiation-belt loss and magnetosphere-ionosphere studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/1R: BARREL-1R was an individual NASA/Dartmouth BARREL high-altitude balloon payload operated in the 2013 Antarctic campaign. It drifted in the Antarctic stratosphere, not in orbit, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation and related magnetospheric activity, with magnetometer, GPS, and engineering data.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/1U: BARREL-1U was an individual NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses payload, operated in 2013 during the first Antarctic BARREL campaign. It flew as a long-duration stratospheric balloon over Antarctica and the Southern Ocean, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays/gamma rays and magnetic field signatures of radiation-belt electron precipitation, often coordinated with Van Allen Probes.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/2Y: BARREL-2Y was a NASA high-altitude balloon payload flown over Antarctica in the 2014 BARREL second campaign, not an orbital spacecraft. It drifted in the stratospheric polar vortex at roughly 30–40 km altitude, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, with magnetometer and GPS context, coordinated with Van Allen Probes.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/1V: BARREL-1V was an individual NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses payload, launched and operated during the 2013 Antarctic stratospheric balloon campaign and ended after that flight. It drifted at long-duration-balloon altitudes over high southern latitudes, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays from precipitating radiation-belt electrons with magnetometer and GPS/ephemeris context.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/3E: BARREL-3E was a NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses payload operated in 2015, launched from Esrange Space Center near Kiruna, Sweden for the northern high-latitude stratospheric balloon campaign. Floating in the Arctic stratosphere, it measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from precipitating radiation-belt electrons, plus magnetic field and GPS/ephemeris data.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/1D: BARREL-1D was a NASA/Dartmouth BARREL stratospheric balloon payload flown during the 2013 Antarctic campaign, drifting at high altitude over Antarctica rather than orbiting Earth. It measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, with magnetometer data, to study substorms and wave-particle interactions in near-Earth space.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/1B: BARREL-1B was one payload in NASA’s Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses, operated during the 2013 Antarctic long-duration balloon campaign. Flying in the stratosphere over Antarctica rather than in orbit, it measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, with magnetometer and GPS/ephemeris data for geospace context.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/4A: BARREL-4A was an individual NASA/Dartmouth BARREL stratospheric balloon payload, operated only during its 2016 Sweden/Arctic flight after launch from Esrange near Kiruna. It drifted at balloon altitude through the polar atmosphere, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays/gamma rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation for Van Allen Probes conjunction and magnetospheric loss studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/1J: BARREL-1J was a NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses high-altitude balloon payload flown over Antarctica during the first BARREL campaign in 2013, ending that year. It drifted in the stratospheric polar vortex and measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, with supporting magnetometer and GPS/housekeeping data.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/BARREL/2F: BARREL-2F was a NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses stratospheric balloon payload, launched and ended in 2014 during the second Antarctic campaign. It drifted over Antarctica rather than orbiting, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation and local magnetic field variations to study electron loss, often with Van Allen Probes context.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/IAGA/Boulder: The Boulder Magnetometer (IAGA code BOU) is a ground geomagnetic observatory near Boulder, Colorado, USA, operational since 1963. It has no orbital phases; it records continuous local vector geomagnetic field variations used to study ionospheric currents, geomagnetic storms, magnetospheric disturbances, and space-weather conditions.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/IAGA/Gillam: Gillam (IAGA GIM/GILL) is a fixed ground magnetometer observatory at Gillam, Manitoba, Canada, operational by the CANOPUS era in 1986 and continuing in CARISMA/INTERMAGNET service. It records vector geomagnetic-field variations for studies of auroral electrojets, substorms, ionospheric currents, and magnetospheric disturbances; its location has not changed.
Cambridge Bay Magnetometer (IAGA CBB) is a fixed ground geomagnetic observatory at Cambridge Bay, Nunavut, Canada, operational since the early 1970s. It measures local magnetic-field variations for studies of auroral electrojets, ionospheric/magnetospheric currents, and geomagnetic disturbances; its location has not changed.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/IAGA/Vostok: Vostok (IAGA code VOS) is a ground geomagnetic observatory at Russia’s Vostok Station in inland East Antarctica (near 78.5°S, 106.9°E), operating from the International Geophysical Year era around 1957–1958 and continuing with possible data gaps. It records geomagnetic field variations for high-latitude ionospheric and magnetospheric studies; as a fixed ground station it has no orbital phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/IAGA/Yellowknif: Yellowknife (YKC) is a fixed ground geomagnetic observatory near Yellowknife, Northwest Territories, Canada, operated in the Canadian/IAGA/INTERMAGNET networks since 1957 and still active. It has no orbit; it measures local vector magnetic-field variations for studies of ionospheric currents, magnetospheric disturbances, substorms, and auroral activity.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/IAGA/Nord: Nord (IAGA code NRD) is a ground-based geomagnetic observatory at Station Nord in northeast Greenland, operational since at least the 1990s. It measures local vector magnetic-field variations for studies of polar ionospheric currents, auroral electrojets, magnetic storms, and magnetosphere–ionosphere coupling, and contributes to IAGA/INTERMAGNET-style geomagnetic networks.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/IAGA/Nurmijarvi: Nurmijärvi (NUR) is a Finnish Meteorological Institute ground geomagnetic observatory in southern Finland (near 60.5°N, 24.7°E), operating since 1953. It has no orbit; it records continuous local vector magnetic-field variations, contributing to IAGA/INTERMAGNET and the IMAGE network for ionospheric, magnetospheric, auroral-electrojet, and space-weather studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/IAGA/Ottawa: Ottawa (OTT) is a ground-based IAGA geomagnetic observatory in Ottawa, Ontario, Canada, operating since 1968. Its magnetometers record local vector geomagnetic field variations for studies of geomagnetic activity, magnetospheric currents, ionospheric disturbances, and space weather, and its data contribute to IAGA/INTERMAGNET-style global observatory networks.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/IAGA/Jan.Mayen: Jan Mayen Magnetometer is a fixed ground geomagnetic observatory on Jan Mayen Island, Norway (about 70.9°N, 8.7°W), with IAGA/CDAWeb digital records in operation by at least the 1990s and continuing in modern archives. It measures vector geomagnetic field variations for high-latitude auroral, ionospheric, and magnetospheric studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/IAGA/Victoria: Victoria (VIC) is an IAGA/Canadian ground geomagnetic observatory operating in Victoria, British Columbia, Canada since 1957. It has no orbit; it records local vector magnetic-field variations and geomagnetic indices/measurements used for ionospheric, magnetospheric, and space-weather studies, with data distributed through systems including CDAWeb.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/IAGA/Oulujarvi: Oulujärvi (OUJ) is a fixed IAGA/IMAGE ground magnetometer station near Oulujärvi in central Finland, operational since 1983 with no orbital phases or relocations. It records three-component geomagnetic field variations for studies of auroral electrojets, ionospheric currents, geomagnetic pulsations, substorms, and magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/IAGA/Poker.Flat: The Poker Flat magnetometer is a ground-based IAGA geomagnetic station at Poker Flat Research Range near Fairbanks, Alaska, operating at least since the 1970s in CDAWeb/IAGA records. It measures local vector geomagnetic-field variations for auroral, ionospheric-current, substorm, and magnetospheric studies; its observing location has not changed.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/IAGA/Brorfelde: Brorfelde (BFE) was an IAGA ground geomagnetic observatory at Brorfelde, Denmark, operated from 1978 until about 2011/2012. It recorded vector and scalar geomagnetic field variations for studies of ionospheric and magnetospheric currents, magnetic storms, secular variation, and global observatory indices; it had no orbital phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/IAGA/Fort.Smith: Fort Smith (FSM) is a ground geomagnetic observatory at Fort Smith, Northwest Territories, Canada, operated since about 1972 as part of the Canadian/IAGA geomagnetic network. It has no orbit; it records vector and scalar geomagnetic-field variations for studies of ionospheric and magnetospheric currents, storms, and substorms.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/IAGA/Tucson: Tucson (TUC) is a ground geomagnetic observatory near Tucson, Arizona, USA, operated in the IAGA/INTERMAGNET network since 1909 and available via CDAWeb. It has no orbit; fixed at its Arizona site, it records vector and scalar variations of Earth’s magnetic field with fluxgate/proton magnetometers for geomagnetic storms, ionospheric currents, and space-weather studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/IAGA/Hankasalmi: Hankasalmi (HAN), operational in the IMAGE ground magnetometer network since the 1990s, is a fixed IAGA station at Hankasalmi, Finland (~62.3°N, 26.6°E). It measures three-component geomagnetic field variations for ionospheric current, auroral electrojet, and magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling studies; it has no orbital phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/IAGA/Fort.Simps: Fort Simpson is a fixed ground-based IAGA magnetometer observatory at Fort Simpson, Northwest Territories, Canada, operational by about 1973 (exact start/end not verified here). It measures local geomagnetic-field variations for auroral electrojet, substorm, magnetic-storm, and high-latitude disturbance studies; it has no orbital phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/IAGA/Baker.Lake: Baker Lake (IAGA code BLC) is a ground-based geomagnetic observatory at Baker Lake, Nunavut, Canada, operating in the IAGA/CDAWeb record since at least the late 1950s. It measures local vector geomagnetic field variations for auroral-zone, magnetospheric, ionospheric, and geomagnetic-storm studies; its location has no orbital phases.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/IAGA/Tromso: Tromsø Magnetometer is a ground-based IAGA geomagnetic observatory at Tromsø, Norway (TRO; ~69.7°N, 19.0°E), operational since the 20th century, with digital CDAWeb-era data used for heliophysics. It measures local geomagnetic field variations from auroral electrojets, ionospheric currents, substorms, and geomagnetic storms; it has no orbital history.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/IAGA/Inuvik: The Inuvik (INK) Magnetic Observatory is a ground-based IAGA/INTERMAGNET geomagnetic station near Inuvik, Northwest Territories, Canada, operating since 1957. It continuously measures Earth’s magnetic field components and total intensity, supporting auroral-zone ionospheric, magnetospheric, geomagnetic-disturbance, and space-weather studies.
spase://SMWG/Observatory/IAGA/Barentsbur: Barentsburg (IAGA code BBG) is a ground-based geomagnetic observatory at Barentsburg, Svalbard, operational by the 1990s and continuing in modern archives. It measures vector geomagnetic field variations in the high-latitude auroral/polar-cap region for studies of ionospheric currents, substorms, magnetic storms, and polar geospace disturbances.
